title: Why did Hegseth face an impeachment push? Inside the 8 articles
summary: The impeachment resolution focuses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky led a now-blocked push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges were laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House voted late Tuesday to refer the resolution to a committee, effectively killing it, after no Republicans joined Massie and House Democrats.

The impeachment resolution focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.
Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:
Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization
The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.
The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.
Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war
The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.
At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.
Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline
The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."
Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."
Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.
Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.
Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.
The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."
Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly
The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."
Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."
Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."
Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.
Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen
The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.
The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.
"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of a week after the election, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — while one Republican won reelection and CBS News estimated four districts with GOP incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

As of Monday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Monday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. In the midterms, both parties won the same number of seats as before, with Democrats winning in all four districts that Republicans had targeted, meaning the redistricting effort did not net the GOP any seats.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Democrats have picked up one other seat, and another race is considered a toss-up.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.
Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: Hegseth decries impeachment effort with vote expected tonight
summary: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie said a vote in the House is expected later Tuesday on the impeachment resolutions against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Update: The House on Tuesday night blocked the effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Read earlier developments below.

Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday defiantly denounced the impeachment effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle" ahead of an expected vote in the House on the measure later in the day.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said.
The defense secretary called Massie's impeachment effort an attempt to harm President Trump because of his own "personal animus" for the president and dislike of the Trump administration's policies.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said.
The House is expected to take up the impeachment resolution Tuesday evening, Massie said, but will likely first hold a procedural vote to table the measure.

In his remarks at the Defense Department, Hegseth claimed that the impeachment effort targeting him is only the first step and will next lead to actions against service members who participated in strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," he said. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."
Hegseth likened the attempt to impeach him to Mr. Trump's two impeachments. While the House voted twice to impeach the president during his first term, he was acquitted both times by the Senate.

"If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week," he said. Hegseth said the House never moved to impeach his predecessor, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, who served during the Biden administration.

Hegseth listed the actions the Defense Department has taken so far during Mr. Trump's second term, including launching military operations against Iran, and hailed the president for demonstrating leadership by going to war with Tehran.

The defense secretary said he has a "ton of support" on Capitol Hill and said Republicans "don't want to vote for something that isn't real," echoing his claim that the articles of impeachment are "flimsy."
Shortly after Hegseth finished his remarks, Mr. Trump praised his Pentagon chief and denounced Massie.
"Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" the president wrote on Truth Social.

The briefing comes one day after Massie introduced updated articles of impeachment against Hegseth. The resolution accuses Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations. Under House rules, the chamber has two legislative days to schedule a vote.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has criticized Hegseth for months. But his renewed impeachment push follows Republicans' sweeping defeats in the midterms, which members of both parties blamed on the Iran war and soaring energy prices. The war's status is unclear: Mr. Trump said Monday he plans to maintain the "status quo" and doesn't believe escalating the war will be necessary.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who represents New York, said Monday afternoon he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment resolution, telling reporters Hegseth "abused his power" and is the "architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran."

It remains to be seen whether Republicans other than Massie will vote in favor of the articles of impeachment. Massie said Monday afternoon he did not have a commitment from any other Republicans that they would support it.

Until Democrats take control of the House in January, any impeachment effort would need support from at least three Republicans — if all Democrats vote in favor and depending on any absences. Removing Hegseth from office by convicting him in the Senate is a much heavier lift, requiring more than a dozen Republicans to join the effort.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told CBS News: "impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now … in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look."
The GOP leader told reporters Tuesday that he expects the House will defeat the impeachment push.
"You don't impeach a Cabinet secretary lightly," Johnson said. "They had no due process. There's nothing that went into this. This is just purely for people to get attention, and it's shameful."

Other Republicans have not definitively ruled it out. Rep. French Hill of Arkansas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend, "I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."

Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a moderate who is retiring in January, said Monday he's "wrestling" with the issue, telling reporters, "I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that?"
Asked by reporters about the impeachment bid, Hegseth said Monday, "We're not worried about that."
In a social media video last week, Hegseth criticized Massie, who is leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.
Mr. Trump told reporters Monday he will stand by Hegseth if he's impeached, defending his Pentagon chief and calling Massie a "stone-cold loser."
"What has Hegseth done?" he said. "Pete Hegseth won two wars. 'Oh, let's impeach him.'"

Massie said Monday: "I would like to see him go through the eight articles of impeachment. Just make the argument from a podium. You can use notes. Get the lawyers to help you. Tell us why you are not guilty of each of these eight articles of impeachment."

title: Sanders won't back Schumer as Democratic leader
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader in the new Congress, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.
story: Washington — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader when the party takes control of the Senate, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.

Sanders made the announcement at a press conference at the Capitol, saying last week's midterm elections were "about change." Democrats will control at least 54 seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

"It was an election across the country, in red states and blue states, where people were looking around them and saying, 'What is going on in America, when I am struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing, and I'm worried not only that my life economically is going nowhere, everything being equal, my kid in the richest country in the history of the world is going to have the lowest standard of living than I do?' And while all of this is going on, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good," Sanders said.

He added: "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, called for "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."
"We need to have that out in the open to show the American people that a new day has come and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington," he said.

Sanders appeared alongside Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said that "whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then in particular how they're going to communicate differently."
Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

No contender has emerged to challenge Schumer's role atop the Senate Democratic caucus, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has come the closest to throwing his hat in the ring. After initially saying he would not pursue the position, Van Hollen has said this week that he's exploring a potential run.
"What I've said from the very beginning is, we shouldn't have a coronation," he said on Monday. "I'm in listening mode and haven't shut the door."
At an event on Tuesday, Van Hollen said he is "in the process right now of calling my colleagues."
"I'm actively calling my colleagues because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus," he said.
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December.

title: 3 Iran-backed operatives indicted for alleged role in terror plots
summary: Three Iran-linked operatives are accused of plotting a terrorist attack at an air base in the U.K. and attempting over a dozen attacks in the U.S. and Europe.
story: Three Iran-backed operatives have been charged with plotting a terrorist attack at a British Royal Air Force base in the United Kingdom where U.S. troops are stationed, the Justice Department announced on Tuesday.

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi was indicted in May on federal charges of conspiracy to provide material support to Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. He is accused in an eight-count superseding indictment made public Tuesday of attempting to coordinate with two other operatives to attack the British Royal Air Force base in the U.K. in September.

Al-Saadi is currently in federal custody in New York. In Tuesday's filing, the Justice Department alleged that he had plotted the air base attack with Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, by "passing them coded messages through third parties."
Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Federal prosecutors allege that beginning in August, Al-Saadi "directed and paid" associates in the United Kingdom to prepare for and arrange an attack at RAF Fairford, including directing an unnamed individual to conduct surveillance at the air base. Al-Saadi then allegedly later paid multiple unnamed people to organize vans and barrels of fuel, and to research chemical accelerants and buy metal to be used as shrapnel for a potential attack.
The indictment alleges that three individuals would then drive the vans, filled with fuel, to RAF Fairford, where they would explode.

Prosecutors say Al-Saadi told the individuals to mark the vans with custom decals to disguise themselves as a fuel delivery or pool supply business and directed his family members to pass messages to his co-conspirators.

In one phone call with his sister from July, Al-Saadi asked his sister to pass on messages to Mohajeri about "work," referring to terrorist activity, and asked if some of their work was canceled or paused.
Al-Saadi's sister replied that the work "isn't cancelled."
On Sept. 24, Al-Saadi allegedly asked how al-Hassani was, and instructed his family to "give him money so we can do it," referring to the RAF Fairford attack.

The indictment then alleges that al-Hassani directed three individuals to drive the vans on Sept. 26 to RAF Fairford. Two of the vans encountered security checkpoints and were not able to proceed on their intended route to the base, the indictment alleges.
Federal prosecutors said that law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three vans with fuel delivery business decals on them and arrested the drivers.

Prosecutors previously alleged that Al-Saadi had plotted to carry out terror attacks in the U.S., including at a prominent Jewish institution in New York. They also accused him of being "involved in the planning, execution and promotion" of approximately 18 reported terror attacks in Europe and two in Canada against U.S. and Israeli interests since March, in retaliation against the U.S. and Israel's military actions in Iran.
In a statement, Attorney General Todd Blanche said "anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

title: House GOP elects Jim Jordan as next leader in major shakeup
summary: Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise for the role of minority leader.
story: Washington — House Republicans voted to elevate Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to lead the party in the next Congress, selecting him over current Majority Leader Steve Scalise following the GOP's crippling losses in last week's midterm elections.

Jordan is a hard-line conservative and close ally of President Trump. His ascension to minority leader represents a significant shakeup for House Republicans, who are looking to rebuild after losing more than 40 House seats.
Tuesday's vote was 106 to 73, sources familiar with the tally told CBS News.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom. And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day," Jordan said in brief remarks after the leadership elections.
House Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping down from leadership and has been noncommittal in recent days about his long-term future in Congress.

Jordan and Scalise both ran for House speaker after Kevin McCarthy's ouster in 2023, leading to weeks of turbulence in the House. But Jordan and Scalise failed to unite the party's various factions. Johnson — who was then a little-known conservative with no leadership experience — pulled off a surprise victory with the conference voting unanimously to make him speaker.
Jordan helped start the conservative House Freedom Caucus and has chaired the House Judiciary Committee since 2023.

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democratic majority," Jordan said in his candidacy letter, arguing that he was "battle-tested."
Scalise, a Louisiana Republican, has held leadership roles since 2014, serving as majority and minority whip before becoming majority leader in 2023.

Scalise was critically injured when a gunman opened fire on a congressional baseball practice in 2017. In 2023, Scalise announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He said several months later that he was in remission after undergoing treatment.
"This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me," Scalise said in his letter to his Republican colleagues announcing his candidacy.

Rounding out the rest of the GOP leadership team is Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip, Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan as conference chair and Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia as chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee.
Emmer and McClain hold the same roles in the majority. Jack will replace Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina as chair of the House GOP's campaign arm. Hudson lost his race for reelection.

title: Thune wins reelection as Senate GOP leader after midterms losses
summary: Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after their brutal midterm losses.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader on Tuesday, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after the party's brutal midterm losses, which saw at least seven Senate seats fall to the Democrats.
Senate Republicans backed Thune for another two years as leader by acclamation, or without opposition, after meeting behind closed doors in the Old Senate Chamber for much of the day.

Thune, 65, is a South Dakota Republican who was first elected leader after the 2024 elections. He's been in the Senate since 2005 and took the helm two decades later, after working under Sen. Mitch McConnell as the No. 2 Senate Republican.
Well-liked by his conference, there was little doubt that Thune would remain leader. But a last-minute push by several conservative members to delay the elections added a wrinkle.

GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin led the push to delay the vote after the disastrous midterm results for Republicans. He secured signatures from a handful of his colleagues — Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah — to compel a conference meeting ahead of Tuesday's elections. But the effort to delay any further fell short.
Johnson told reporters that Senate Republicans "just can't continue on business as usual" after a "stunning defeat" at the polls.
"I mean, that kind of defeat demands change," Johnson said, when asked whether new leadership was needed.
But Johnson conceded that there wasn't a clear alternative to Thune. He argued that Senate Republicans at least needed to hear from their leadership team about the strategy moving forward.
After meeting behind closed doors for two hours Tuesday morning, and reconvening later in the afternoon, Johnson told reporters that "this has never been anything against John Thune."
"I think he has been very unfairly attacked by our base," Johnson said.
For his part, Thune appeared sympathetic to the efforts to regroup, and he acknowledged that the decision over whether to delay selecting their leaders would ultimately come down to members.

"I think in the end, I think it's important that for purposes of moving forward, that we get some of these issues settled as soon as possible," Thune told CBS News on Monday. "We'll see what our members think tomorrow."

Thune's reelection as leader comes after he led Senate Republicans as they passed the president's massive tax, border security and defense agenda, swiftly confirmed the president's nominees, and approved a handful of bipartisan priorities over the last two years. At the same time, his tenure was marked by two record-breaking government shutdowns, and a White House that often moved out of step with Republicans in Congress.

Some Republicans were critical of Thune's record, arguing that the GOP agenda wasn't aggressive enough. Conservative frustrations came to a head over the SAVE America Act, a controversial election bill that President Trump repeatedly pushed. Thune made clear that the legislation did not enjoy enough support in the upper chamber to move forward.

Ahead of the election, Thune pushed back on the criticism about the Senate GOP agenda, telling CBS News, "I don't know how you could be more aggressive." And he defended Senate Republicans' record, while acknowledging that there were factors beyond their control.

Senate Republicans had entered the midterm cycle with a map that initially looked favorable, offering few pickup opportunities for Democrats. But GOP candidates across the country were routed as cost of living concerns and the war in Iran took center stage, and expanded the map for Democrats. The Senate GOP lost seats in battleground states like Ohio and North Carolina, along with Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. Two Senate contests — Alaska and Mississippi — remain unresolved, and could yield more victories for Democrats.

Thune, in his first floor speech since the midterms, said, "There is no doubt about it, Tuesday night was a tough election night." He said the election results gave Senate Republicans "an opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do better" and "a clear message that this coming Congress needs to double down on the work that we've been doing on affordability."

title: Judge denounces DOJ lawsuit over California mail ballots
summary: The Justice Department unsuccessfully attempted to force California election workers to set aside mail ballots returned from up to 20,000 alleged noncitizens.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday condemned a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to force California to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 alleged noncitizens as an attempt to "disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty."

The one-paragraph order from U.S. District Judge David Carter came in response to the Trump administration's move to voluntarily dismiss the suit it filed against California officials and Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, just weeks before the midterm elections.

"This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike," Carter wrote. "The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy."

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit after alleging that there were more than 20,000 people who it believed were not U.S. citizens but were registered to vote in California. It sought a court order forcing election workers to separate mail ballots returned by those it had identified as suspected noncitizens.
The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, after voting in California had begun and after hundreds of thousands of mail ballots had already been returned to election offices.

Carter, appointed by former President Bill Clinton, rejected the Trump administration's effort to require election workers to put aside those ballots and not count them until voters' citizenship could be verified. After failing to secure similar relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and the Supreme Court before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the Justice Department notified Carter on Saturday that it would be dismissing the case.

"In light of the Supreme Court's denial, the United States is evaluating how to best ensure that American votes are protected, including by preventing vote dilution by noncitizens," a Justice Department lawyer wrote in a filing.

The Trump administration said that by the time of the court's next hearing in the case, set for Friday, "California will have already commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones. There is then no way to get the challenged ballots segregated. As a result, the relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary."
In his brief order, Carter officially closed the case and canceled Friday's hearing.

title: Inside the unconventional tenure of Stanley Woodward, DOJ's No. 3
summary: Observers say Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward has carved out an unusual role, with a pattern of intervening in pending criminal cases involving corporations.
story: Washington — In an address to some members of the Justice Department's Antitrust Division in October, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward made an unusual pitch.

He wanted to entice the lawyers there to leave their roles and accept temporary stints to help out the National Fraud Enforcement Division, created earlier this year, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the speech.

In a 30-minute talk, he criticized the federal judge overseeing a lawsuit over President Trump's plans to renovate a public golf course in Washington, and told the group to come to him if they ever have a problem with a judge in the future.
But before he could finish his address, he abruptly left, saying he was getting a call from the president.
The speech offered a glimpse of the unusual role Woodward has carved out as the No. 3 official at the Justice Department.

Since taking office last fall, he has become the de facto leader of the Antitrust Division, put his name on controversial court filings that have bewildered some DOJ employees and voiced a strong philosophical opposition to prosecuting corporations that has shocked many inside the department, multiple sources told CBS News.

Observers say he has developed a pattern of intervening in pending criminal cases involving corporations that are being pursued by the divisions under his remit, often steering them against the recommendations of career prosecutors and even other political appointees.

One example, which has not been previously reported, involved an Illinois mining company that allegedly failed to evacuate its employees during a 2021 fire and failed to report another blaze to regulators as recently as this year, multiple sources told CBS News.
Woodward's defenders describe him as smart, deeply engaged and willing to take the hits that come with leadership.
A Justice Department spokesperson acknowledged Woodward urged antitrust attorneys to take assignments in the new fraud division, saying some of them have relevant experience.
The spokesperson did not dispute the account of Woodward's remarks — or the fact they were interrupted by a call from the White House.
"It is well known that Woodward was an advisor to the President prior to coming over to DOJ," the spokesperson said.
This account of Woodward's tenure is based on interviews with nearly two dozen people, all of whom asked to remain anonymous to candidly discuss internal deliberations or cases.
The Justice Department did not make Woodward available for an interview.

"The notion that the No. 3 person at the Department of Justice doesn't believe in the criminal prosecution of corporations is purely an ideological oddity unsupported by law," said one person familiar with Woodward's views. "It is a fact that in multiple situations, he has asked prosecutors to justify prosecutions against companies."
"You can't put a company in jail"

Woodward has less experience with criminal matters than he does with civil litigation. From 2010 to 2020, he was an associate and senior counsel at the law firm Akin Gump, where he primarily worked on civil matters.

The corporate criminal cases he did work on largely played out behind the scenes, two people familiar with his workload said, making it hard to get a full window into his experience. Most of them involved investigations under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, they said, a law that prohibits foreign bribery. He cited one such case on a Senate questionnaire when asked to list the 10 most significant cases of his career, saying he spent six months overseeing a team of lawyers who reviewed documents.

In 2020, he and Stan Brand, a former general counsel for the House of Representatives, started a law firm together. Over the next five years, he represented a number of criminal defendants in Mr. Trump's orbit, including Walt Nauta and Peter Navarro. He was also counsel to Kelly Meggs, a member of the far-right Oath Keepers who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, and was convicted on multiple felonies, including seditious conspiracy. His sentence was later commuted by Mr. Trump.
While all of the clients he represented during that time who went to trial lost their cases, at least some of the judges in federal court in D.C. seemed to respect him as an attorney.

"The district judges down there loved him," said one person with knowledge of the cases he handled. "He wasn't one of those goofy Trump lawyers. He was a by-the-book defense guy. They liked him because he knew what he was doing."

He briefly worked in the White House as a senior counselor to the president before joining the Justice Department in April 2025 as an aide to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. He was elevated to associate attorney general that October.

The job of associate attorney general primarily entails overseeing the Justice Department's civil side: divisions that handle civil rights, antitrust probes, environmental and animal welfare issues, civil enforcement actions, civil tax cases and the offices that defend the government in civil lawsuits. Several of those divisions also have sections that prosecute crimes like price-fixing, air and water pollution violations, and civil rights offenses.

While the majority of his day-to-day job involves civil matters, he has made waves internally when it comes to how he views the smaller subset of corporate criminal cases that fall under his remit, multiple sources said.

In meetings with DOJ attorneys to discuss pending cases, he has been known to often quip that "you can't put a company in jail" or that there is "no jail big enough for a corporation," according to multiple sources, including some eyewitnesses.
He also frequently advocates for prosecutors to seek softer resolutions, such as deferred prosecution agreements or civil settlements in lieu of criminal charges, the sources said.
"He openly shows disdain toward every corporate case," recalled one person who said they have heard Woodward express those sentiments on more than one occasion.
"The impression you get is he doesn't believe in any of these laws and he does not believe in prosecuting companies at all," the person added.

His strong views on corporate prosecutions in general — essentially that they shouldn't happen — have shocked many attorneys at the Justice Department, particularly coming from an office that historically has not been heavily involved in scrutinizing criminal cases, since most of that oversight falls to the office of the deputy attorney general.
They also stand in stark contrast to how most of his predecessors viewed such cases, and even many of his fellow Trump appointees inside the department.

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, for instance, recently ordered prosecutors in the National Fraud Enforcement Division to "zealously prosecute corporate actors that defraud taxpayers and the United States of America."

On several occasions, Woodward has asked prosecutors to write memos explaining basic legal principles related to prosecuting companies, in what they saw as a sign that he does not have very much experience with corporate criminal work, several sources with knowledge of the requests told CBS News.

In one example, he asked prosecutors to explain the basic "blackletter law" outlining how the Justice Department can even charge a company, one person recalled. The authority to do so was affirmed in a landmark 1909 Supreme Court case which held that companies can be held criminally liable for unlawful acts carried out by personnel acting within the scope of their employment.

Another time, Woodward asked antitrust prosecutors to draft a memo explaining the difference between the "per se rule" and the "rule of reason," sources with knowledge of the request said. The former is a legal doctrine that DOJ has historically relied upon to criminally prosecute inherently illegal acts like bid-rigging. The latter is a different analytical legal standard that DOJ often applies in most civil antitrust enforcement cases.
A Justice Department spokesperson said Woodward "does not support new and novel theories of prosecution against companies or individuals."

"But that doesn't mean companies that break the law should go free writ large — his view is that it's individuals who break the law and so prosecuting individuals for criminal conduct should always be prioritized," the spokesperson added.
The clearest recent example of his approach involves M-Class Mining LLC, the Illinois mining company.

A subsidiary of Foresight Energy, M-Class Mining allegedly failed to evacuate its employees during an August 2021 underground fire or alert federal regulators. An indictment in August charged four executives with conspiring to defraud the U.S. and other counts, including obstruction.

Senior political and career officials from the Labor Department and Justice Department had all expressed support for charging the company itself after determining it was plagued by a problematic corporate culture that, in their belief, was not solely caused by a few rogue actors, sources said. Among the aggravating factors was the fact that the company later rehired as a mine safety consultant one of its employees who allegedly obstructed the government.

At first, prosecutors had a green light to pursue a prosecution of the corporation. But Woodward overruled recommendations from both career and Trump-appointed attorneys involved in the investigation.

At one point, Woodward and officials in the deputy attorney general's office contemplated a deferred prosecution agreement as an alternative, after speaking with the company's lawyer, Ed O'Callaghan, a former DOJ official who served during Mr. Trump's first term, sources told CBS News.

But allowing the company to dodge charges through a deferred prosecution agreement ran afoul of the Justice Department's new corporate charging policy. The policy allows firms to avoid criminal charges if they self-report the violations, cooperate with the government and work to remediate compliance problems.

Officials expressed concerns because the company did not qualify for a deferred prosecution under the policy, and because such agreements were meant to be reserved for companies that tried to remedy compliance problems and cooperate in good faith, one of the sources added.

In the end, the Justice Department took no action against M-Class Mining itself, instead indicting four individuals who worked for the company with conspiring to defraud the government. Some also faced additional charges of falsifying records and obstruction.
An agreement to pause the statute of limitations expired at the end of October, making criminal charges against the corporation now impossible.
O'Callaghan declined to comment, and said the company also declined to comment.
Despite Woodward's overall lack of enthusiasm on pursuing corporate criminal cases, some say they have appreciated his general willingness to advocate for prosecutors to move more quickly.

At the start of most meetings, in fact, he likes to remind people of how many days remain in the Trump administration, pushing them to get results, according to sources who have been in meetings with him.
"He likes to be viewed as a bear you don't want to poke," one person who worked closely with him said.
The "Stanley-only brief"

The No. 3 official at the Justice Department has historically drawn less attention than the attorney general and deputy attorney general, but Woodward has made headlines in ways his predecessors have not.
One of the most striking aspects of his tenure is his willingness to put his signature on a number of unusual and controversial legal filings that make many of his colleagues uncomfortable.

Earlier this year, Woodward was the sole DOJ signatory on a settlement between the president and the IRS which called for the creation of a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" that would be used to provide payouts to those who could show they had been wrongfully targeted by the government. It was widely seen as an effort to distribute money to Jan. 6 defendants and other Trump allies who had been investigated or charged under the Biden administration.

Woodward had represented several would-be claimants to the fund, a fact that prompted a federal judge in Florida to rebuke him in a scathing court ruling. The judge sent a copy of her opinion to the District of Columbia bar, where Woodward is licensed. A nonprofit watchdog group filed a separate bar complaint.
Gene Rossi, a defense attorney who worked closely with Woodward on a separate Oath Keepers trial, said he was "always professional and very gifted."

"But am I disappointed in what he is doing today? Absolutely yes," Rossi said. "My respect for Stanley Woodward really took a hit when he negotiated that IRS settlement … It was such an easy call ethically to recuse yourself."
Woodward has recently drawn the ire of Judge Ana Reyes, who is overseeing the ongoing civil litigation over Mr. Trump's plans to renovate East Potomac Golf Links in D.C.
On Oct. 16, Woodward was the sole signatory on a brief that accused the judge of bias and demanded she recuse herself from the case.

He also contended in a separate brief on Oct. 18 that the court had no jurisdiction on the case, saying the redesign of the golf course was not a "final agency action." At a hearing the next day, Reyes asked other DOJ attorneys in the courtroom if they would be willing to refile the brief with their signatures on it, a request she later dropped.
Since then, Reyes has raised questions about whether government lawyers and officials intentionally misled her, and appointed a special master to help determine whether they engaged in misconduct.

The pleadings have privately embarrassed both political appointees and career attorneys in the Justice Department, and also baffled people who know Woodward well and have respect for him as an attorney, multiple sources with direct knowledge of the dynamic said. When Woodward is the sole signature on a brief, it is usually a safe bet that no one else in the department was willing to sign it, the people said.
"A Stanley-only brief is a sure sign that everyone else refused, or he knew everyone would refuse and didn't even ask," one of those people said.

In April, Woodward signed and submitted two briefs defending Mr. Trump's plans to construct a new ballroom at the White House from a suit by a historic preservation group. Both included language that mimicked the style and tone of the president's Truth Social posts. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter's names also appeared on the briefs, which did not include any career officials.

"'The National Trust for Historic Preservation' is a beautiful name, but even their name is FAKE because when they add the words 'in the United States' to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, it makes it sound like a Governmental Agency, which it is not," one of the filings said, accusing the group of "Trump Derangement Syndrome."
One person who has worked with Woodward said that his willingness to sign certain filings is a sign of his leadership.

"He didn't have to sign that brief. He easily could have ordered someone else to do it, but he recognizes that sometimes when you're the leader, you need to be out in front taking the hits," the person said.
A Justice Department spokesperson said that Woodward only signs briefs that he believes are righteous.

Woodward "doesn't sign things he does not believe can be filed in good faith. He reads everything that he signs personally," the spokesperson said, adding that "zealous advocacy should not be confused with 'combativeness.'"
"Courts of appeals and the Supreme Court exist to affirm or overturn decisions of a lower court," the spokesperson added.
The fact that the associate attorney general is signing briefs in court at all is a surprise to some veteran DOJ attorneys, who say it is not customary practice.

"I can't think of a single case during either of my stints in the Civil Rights Division where the associate AG was the only person who signed a court filing," said Pamela Karlan, a former principal deputy assistant attorney general who now teaches law at Stanford. "In fact, I can't remember a case — outside of a couple of cases at the Supreme Court, maybe — where anyone from the associate attorney general's office appeared on the briefing. And there were always career lawyers on every filing."
The Antitrust Division
Another unusual aspect of Woodward's tenure is the extent to which he is overseeing the Antitrust Division.

Last year, Woodward and Chad Mizelle, then Bondi's chief of staff, fired two deputies of antitrust chief Abigail Slater after she pushed back on a settlement clearing Hewlett Packard Enterprise's $14 billion acquisition of Juniper Networks. One of them, Roger Alford, later said in a speech that Woodward and Mizelle had "perverted justice" by letting "lawyers and influence peddlers" shape antitrust outcomes.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on Alford's allegations, saying the department would not respond to "outlandish complaints" from a "disgruntled former employee."
Slater herself was fired less than a year later amid continuing clashes with Woodward and Bondi's offices over antitrust cases.

Before her ouster, Bondi and Woodward tried to keep her from attending a meeting of antitrust regulators under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, or OECD. The Antitrust Division's assistant attorney general customarily attends such meetings, and in that case, Slater was the chair of the group's competition committee.

Department leadership said the trip would violate its travel rules and cut off Slater's credit cards while she was overseas, CBS News previously reported. Sources said she was staying in a government-approved hotel and flew to Paris on a commercial flight.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the attorney general — and not the associate attorney general — had the authority to approve or deny travel requests.

The acting assistant attorney general who followed her left in June. At the OECD's next antitrust meeting, the department sent a lawyer who had worked in Woodward's office, and not anyone from the Antitrust Division, to represent the DOJ, sources with direct knowledge of the arrangement said.
Now, without anyone left to serve as acting assistant attorney general of the Antitrust Division, Woodward has been left to serve as its de facto leader.
A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed that Woodward has been delegated the authorities of the assistant attorney general, though he is technically not serving in that role.

He has consolidated control. He's now in charge of signing off on all administrative subpoenas, known as "civil investigative demands," that the Justice Department uses to compel the production of documents, sources said. Having someone at his level signing off on all those documents is unprecedented, sources with knowledge of the division said, noting that such demands are required by statute to be approved by the assistant attorney general.

His insistence on signing off on other moves, including appellate decisions, has started to cause gridlock in the Antitrust Division, multiple sources said. Some people have resorted to bringing in books to read in the office because their work has slowed so much.
"He is exercising outsized power," said one former official who is familiar with how the Antitrust Division is customarily run. Another source described the dynamics in a similar way.
"It's just a desire to have control of all aspects of the division's activities," the person said.
But what some people see as micromanagement, others see as an example of an associate attorney general who, unlike his predecessors, has taken on a more proactive oversight function.

"Stanley is incredibly smart and deeply engaged. I don't think there has ever been an associate attorney general that has ever been more engaged than Stanley," said another person who has worked directly with Woodward.
A Justice Department spokesperson said that Woodward, as associate attorney general, has oversight authority of Antitrust and has been playing the role for over eight months.

"He has played an oversight and leadership role in ensuring affordability for all Americans with much of the operations and decisions of the Antitrust Division already requiring the Associate's involvement and approval. The Associate Attorney General is best equipped to provide interim leadership over the Antitrust Division to ensure continuity and promised progress in protecting competition for American consumers," the spokesperson added.
The art of Woodward's deal

While Woodward has expressed disdain for corporate criminal cases, he has also demonstrated an eagerness to ratchet up the fines and penalties against corporations when it comes to civil enforcement matters.

In some cases, he has pushed DOJ attorneys in settlement talks to go back to a company and tell them that the government was increasing the amount of money that would be needed to resolve the case — an uncommon tactic.
"He can be pretty aggressive on the civil side," one person told CBS News, adding that Woodward is viewed as "quirky and unpredictable."
In some cases that could be potentially handled both criminally or civilly, Woodward has often advocated for civil resolutions.

"He fancies himself a savvy negotiator," another person noted, saying there have been several occasions where Woodward has offered to obtain a high monetary penalty if lawyers working on the case would let him negotiate a civil resolution in lieu of a criminal one.
One such example played out with parallel criminal and civil investigations into the private equity giant KKR.

In January 2025, shortly before the Trump administration took office, the Justice Department filed a civil complaint alleging the company repeatedly made false statements and omitted key pieces of information at least 16 times in its pre-merger applications, known as Hart-Scott-Rodino filings.

Federal prosecutors in the Antitrust Division also believed the evidence was strong enough to pursue a separate criminal investigation, according to several sources familiar with the matter and a September 2024 corporate filing from KKR disclosing the receipt of a grand jury subpoena.
Initially, prosecutors got a green light from senior political appointees under the Trump administration to continue with the criminal investigation.

But Woodward opposed pursuing a criminal case, one of those sources said. Separately, one of KKR's two chief executives separately complained to the White House about the case, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
After that, prosecutors were ordered to drop the criminal probe before it ever got far enough to know whether charges could be warranted, one of the sources added.

In August, the Justice Department reached a civil settlement with the company for $250 million — an amount that the DOJ touted as being the "largest ever penalty" for violations of a law known as the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act.
Woodward lauded the settlement, saying in a statement that it sent "a powerful message" that the Justice Department is "committed to vigorous enforcement."
KKR declined to comment beyond its prior statement, in which it said it had  "agreed to a civil settlement that fully resolves the litigations and all open investigations by the Antitrust Division."

"We strongly disagree with the Antitrust Division's characterization of this matter.  We believe that our firm acted in good faith at all times under our prior filing process, and that it was consistent with industry practice," the company said.

Ironically, when Woodward made his first appearance at a press conference at the Justice Department as associate attorney general, it was to announce a superseding indictment in a corporate antitrust case involving several Chinese shipping container companies.
The indictment charged both individuals and the corporate entities, alleging they engaged in illegal price fixing during the pandemic.
"We are holding these Chinese bad actors accountable for exploiting the pandemic to fill their own coffers," Woodward said at the time.
The indictment was originally returned in December 2025 — just about two months into Woodward's tenure as associate attorney general.
Unlike some of the other corporate criminal cases, sources said the Chinese containers case did not draw any opposition from Woodward, who even joked that the staff had "snuck one past" him.

United States Department of Justice
United States Department of Justice

title: House finds "decades-long failures" as Epstein preyed on victims
summary: The 15-month investigation by the House Oversight Committee involved interviews with some of Jeffrey Epstein's most high-powered associates.
story: The federal government failed for decades to stop Jeffrey Epstein as he manipulated and sexually abused young women and girls, despite growing evidence of his crimes, according to a report released Tuesday by Republicans on the House Oversight Committee.

The 15-month investigation involved 19 transcribed interviews with witnesses, including some of Epstein's most high-powered associates, and reviews of financial records, Justice Department documents and files from Epstein's estate.

"At nearly every stage, the cases reviewed by the Committee raise troubling questions about how Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, who sexually abused and trafficked young women and girls, avoided accountability for so long," the committee's majority wrote. Maxwell is a former socialite and convicted child sex trafficker who was among Epstein's closest confidants.

The committee's Republicans wrote that Epstein targeted vulnerable young women and girls, promising "career opportunities and comfort until the survivors of his crimes became completely dependent and subservient." Along the way, those around him "seemed to have simply blindly obeyed" as he manipulated the young women.
The committee's top Democrat, Robert Garcia, criticized the report, saying it's "based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings."

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation. We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started," Garcia said in a statement to press.

The report concluded that a "willful ignorance" extended from Epstein's closest employees — his longtime lawyer, accountant and personal assistant, who combined carried out the nitty gritty details of arranging daily massages and managing his "black book" of names — to Epstein's most powerful friends, "who, in the face of numerous red flags, claimed that they never suspected Epstein was abusing women or committing crimes of any kind."
But a willingness to allow Epstein's behavior to continue extended to the federal government itself, they wrote.

Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida state court in 2008 to two prostitution charges, including one count of soliciting prostitution from someone under 18. The report claims that this "sweetheart deal" allowed Epstein to avoid a more sweeping federal case, and may have resulted from conflicts of interest at the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, which ultimately decided against pushing federal charges.

During Epstein's short stint in state custody, he was granted extensive work-release for what the committee called a "sham company." During that time, he continued to abuse women, the committee wrote. Several survivors said they were abused during that time, "in his South Florida office, his Palm Beach residence, or even, in [Sarah] Kellen's case, over video from the stockade itself."

Epstein's fortune was enabled by a cadre of extraordinarily wealthy and powerful clients and friends. The committee interviewed, among others, billionaires Leon Black, Bill Gates, Les Wexner and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. They all said they had no knowledge of Epstein's crimes.

"Some Epstein associates questioned by the Committee seemingly claimed in their testimonies that a man with connections to global political leaders, major philanthropists, titans of industry, billionaires, Hollywood celebrities, and even a British prince could not be a sex trafficker," the committee wrote. "However, despite the repeated assertions of ignorance to Epstein's crimes, these same associates offered inadequate explanations for their continued close association with Epstein after his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor."
Black recently sued the committee's lead Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia, claiming defamation and accusing Garcia of lying about Black's relationship with Epstein.
Garcia said he intends to continue the investigation after Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"The Department of Justice continues to illegally withhold over 2.5 million pages of documents, there's been no investigation of Ghislaine Maxwell's transfer, and Attorney General Todd Blanche has yet to testify about his role in the largest government cover-up of the modern era," Garcia said, referring to the Justice Department's decision to move Maxwell to a minimum-security facility days after Blanche interviewed her. At the time, Blanche was deputy attorney general. It is extraordinarily unusual for Justice Department officials with that seniority to interview inmates.

The report's authors recommendations include encouraging the Justice Department pursue new investigations in Epstein's circle, and that Congress pass legislation to "prevent the weaponization of nondisclosure agreements to silence survivors of sexual abuse."

title: Where the Trump administration's lawsuits seeking voter data stand
summary: The Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over their unredacted voter rolls containing voters' sensitive information.
story: Washington — President Trump's administration has mounted efforts in nearly all 50 states to obtain their complete voter rolls containing sensitive information about registered voters in their states.

The Justice Department has argued that the information is needed to ensure states are complying with two federal voting laws, the Help America Vote Act and the National Voter Registration Act, which aim to ensure states have programs in place for maintaining accurate voter rolls.

The administration sent letters to most of the states last year seeking unredacted electronic copies of their statewide voter registration lists, which include voters' birthdates, addresses, partial Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers.

A number of states have turned over publicly available versions of their voter rolls, but have declined to provide their complete lists. In response, the Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over the voter data.
So far, the Trump administration has lost 28 of those cases. Federal judges have rejected the Justice Department's lawsuits for unredacted voter rolls from:

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's initial case against Georgia because it was filed in the wrong court, and government lawyers then refiled it. The Justice Department voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against Oklahoma after the state agreed to turn over its voter registration list.
The other cases remain pending. Those are in Hawaii and Idaho.

The Justice Department has appealed most of the decisions dismissing its cases. So far, one appeals court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, has upheld a lower court decision rejecting the administration's attempt to obtain Michigan's voter rolls.

The Trump administration's bids to gain access to states' unredacted voter registration lists are part of the president's efforts to exert more power over federal elections. Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders aimed at U.S. elections, though both have been blocked by the courts.

The first executive order, signed last year, would require documentary proof of citizenship in order to register to vote. The second, announced in March, tightens the rules for mail-in voting and requires the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Postal Service to compile and maintain lists of U.S. citizens who are eligible to vote.
Mr. Trump is also pushing Congress to enact a package of voting regulations called the SAVE America Act, which would significantly curtail mail-in voting and impose new voter ID requirements.

The president has long taken aim at mail-in voting and claimed it leads to widespread fraud, though he has not put forth evidence in support of those claims. He has also claimed that Democratic states allow noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote.

title: California voters reject billionaire wealth tax, CBS News projects
summary: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.
story: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.

Proposition 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion, excluding real estate and certain retirement assets. Proponents of the measure said it was expected to generate $100 billion over five years, with 90% going toward healthcare programs and the other 10% for education, food assistance, and administration of the tax.
The proposal came at a time when other states and federal policymakers are debating how to tax extreme wealth and finance public services, and how Proposition 40 was viewed as a bellwether.
The vote was framed by supporters as part of a broader struggle over economic inequality and the political influence of the billionaire class.

Supporters say the state needs additional money to help offset federal healthcare cuts implemented in 2025 under H.R. 1, known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," and to protect hospitals, emergency rooms, clinics and Medi-Cal services. Proponents also argue that billionaires can accumulate substantial wealth from the stock market and business valuations without paying income tax on those gains until they are realized. They also contend that those who have benefited the most from the state's robust economy should contribute more toward public services.

The measure created a divide among politicians and organizations that ordinarily align with Democratic priorities. While it was supported by the California Democratic Party and labor unions including SEIU Healthcare Workers West, the principal sponsor of the measure, it was opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Orange County Rep. Katie Porter, and major healthcare and professional organizations such as the California Medical Association and California Teachers Association.

Newsom and Porter, who have both supported higher taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals, agree with the argument that the proposal would encourage wealthy residents to leave the state and damage its long-term fiscal position by decreasing its tax revenue.

Newsom has also expressed a preference for taxing billionaires at the federal level and says a California-only wealth tax would be limited to funding healthcare and not other needs. Opponents of the measure also claim that the initiative does not provide guarantees about how the money would be allocated among providers and services.

A coalition of billionaires organized in opposition to the measure, such as Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, venture capitalist John Doerr, PayPal and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison.

Wealthy opponents contributed tens of millions of dollars to defeat Prop. 40, with most of the money going to the group Building a Better California, which has raised over $250 million in the campaign against the billionaire tax as of Oct. 28. The funding also went toward supporting two competing measures, Propositions 41 and 42, which would place limits on special taxes and could prevent the billionaire tax from taking effect if either receives more votes than Prop. 40.

A Stanford University study indicated that billionaires who have already left the state, including Brin, Page, and Thiel, have removed about $540 billion, or 30%, of California's billionaire wealth from potential taxation. The study also concluded that Prop. 40 may generate only about $30 billion instead of the $100 billion estimated by its proponents.

Other economists, including Nobel Prize winners Daron Acemoglu of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Joseph Stiglitz of Columbia University, supported the measure, saying that California has attracted more venture funding since Prop. 40 was introduced. An open letter from the economists noted that between 2019 and 2025, the California income tax paid by billionaires was "only 1.6% of their $1.4 trillion wealth gain, much less than what ordinary Californians pay on their paychecks."
One California billionaire who did support Prop. 40 is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose estimated net worth is about $200 billion.

"I don't mind paying taxes; the more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I'm okay with that," Huang told CBS News. "I don't like tax dollars wasted. But I also support all that this country represents."
