title: First snow of the season is coming to Northeast
summary: Parts of the Northeast could see their first snowfall of the season later this week, as a cold snap spreads over the eastern half of the U.S.
story: The first snowfall of the season is expected in parts of the Northeast later this week, although there is uncertainty over how much snow will fall and which parts of the region will be hit hardest.
Temperatures are also forecast to drop well below average for this time of year in that region and other parts of the eastern U.S., impacting a large swath of the country.
Cold snap to spread over eastern U.S. this week

A large dip in the jet stream will cause cold air to spread across the eastern half of the U.S. starting Wednesday through the end of the week, reaching from the Canadian border to the Gulf Coast. Temperatures are expected to drop between 20 and 25 degrees below average for this time of year.

Overnight feels-like temperatures are forecast to be near or below freezing in major cities, including Chicago and Atlanta. Daytime highs will only reach the mid-30s and 40s from Thursday through the upcoming weekend.
Snowfall potential
A separate storm system developing over the Midwest on Wednesday will strengthen and head to the Northeast before the end of the week, potentially helping usher in the first snowfall of the season.

Some of the moisture associated with the storm will fall as cold rain, which is expected in cities like Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Washington, D.C., even though the I-95 corridor will likely see warmer temperatures this weekend.
But places at higher elevations and those in the interior Northeast, like upstate New York, New Hampshire and Vermont, could see their first snowfall.

The storm is expected to move away from land once it reaches the Mid-Atlantic region. A second, smaller storm could potentially form off of that system and impact coastal areas from the Mid-Atlantic up to New England. The path of the second, smaller storm will determine how much snow or rain may fall in those areas, and exactly which locations could be affected.

title: Nvidia's trillion-dollar bind: Can it afford to lose Jensen Huang?
summary: Other CEOs have been ousted over undisclosed relationships, but Nvidia's inquiry shines a spotlight on how closely the chipmaker's fortunes are tied to its co-founder.
story: Nvidia's board of directors faces a trillion-dollar dilemma: Can the chipmaker afford to part with its storied co-founder and CEO, now embroiled in multiple investigations into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy?

In recent years, several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, including former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook and Kohl's CEO Ashley Buchanan. But none is so closely identified with their companies as Huang. Over more than three decades, he has led Nvidia as it grew into one of the world's most valuable companies, with many investors viewing him as equally critical to the company's success as Elon Musk is to SpaceX or Steve Jobs was to Apple.

Huang is facing serious challenges, including an independent inquiry by Nvidia's board into the affair, a shareholder lawsuit and questions from lawmakers. Heightening the stakes are allegations that Huang had a close relationship with a former female executive at an Nvidia customer who is also suspected of working with China's intelligence agency.
$450 billion drop
Nvidia shareholders have been spooked by the disclosure, with the company's shares shedding 10% of their value — or about $450 billion — in the last two trading days alone.
"It exposes how dependent the company is on this one person," Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.
He added, "This is like asking if something happens to Elon Musk, what happens to Tesla and SpaceX's valuations? If something happens to Jensen Huang, what happens to Nvidia's valuation?"

Yorkville Ives tech analyst Dan Ives estimated in a research note that Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its valuation if Huang is removed from his role, while noting that for now most investors expect the executive to retain his post at the company.

"At the end of the day, there is only one Jensen, and Nvidia will dramatically change as a company if he is no longer CEO, with a major negative ripple impact across the tech industry and AI Revolution," Ives said.
"Do not proceed"

Corporate governance experts said Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang — a Chinese executive linked to the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia — appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether Huang had violated any company rules. In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and he apologized for hurting her and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

But Huang's conduct "is definitely a violation," said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, a consulting firm that advises small and midsize businesses on issues including governance. "How he handled it based on their code of conduct is where you're going to see continued issues."
Still, while Huang may have violated company rules, he may be given more leeway than other employees due to his importance to Nvidia, governance experts said.

"This is an outlier — I don't remember a case like this," Columbia's Rajgopal said. "This company is so important to the U.S. in terms of AI, especially with China and other powers. So even if there is a violation of the code of conduct, if I were the chair of the board, I would not dismiss him."

Nvidia's 11-person board includes Huang, although the other board members are considered independent, according to a company regulatory filing. They include California Institute of Technology professor John Dabiri and former Taco Bell International president Melissa Lora. All board members except Dabiri have experience in corporate governance, the filing states.
Nvidia board members should demonstrate their independence by hiring a law firm to help with the investigation, and immediately develop a succession plan for Huang, Rajgopal said.
A common issue for Nvidia and other big tech companies led by their founders is that they are often run "like a family affair," he added.
"These are effectively run like family private companies, but they are mega-cap public companies where most of the capital comes from the public," Rajgopal said. "There is a duty above and beyond."
Succession planning

Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the center of decision-making at Nvidia. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace him remains unclear, heightening pressure on the board, experts said.

"The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options — Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed, and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.
Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

"I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.

title: Why did Hegseth face an impeachment push? Inside the 8 articles
summary: The impeachment resolution focuses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky led a now-blocked push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges were laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House voted late Tuesday to refer the resolution to a committee, effectively killing it, after no Republicans joined Massie and House Democrats.

The impeachment resolution focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.
Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:
Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization
The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.
The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.
Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war
The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.
At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.
Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline
The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."
Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."
Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.
Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.
Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.
The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."
Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly
The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."
Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."
Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."
Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.
Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen
The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.
The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.
"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

title: State seeks to block Pike's lawyers from inspecting execution drug
summary: Tennessee is seeking to block Christa Pike's attorneys from accessing the pentobarbital used in the 50-year-old inmate's botched execution on the grounds that it would reveal the supplier.
story: Tennessee is seeking to block Christa Pike's attorneys from accessing the lethal injection drug used in her failed execution on the grounds that it would reveal the supplier in violation of state law, court filings show.

The request follows a judge's order to preserve evidence in a lawsuit filed by Pike's attorneys and reflects the secrecy surrounding execution drugs, which states often argue is necessary to protect access to the drugs and the safety of suppliers.

Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital in September, which her attorneys say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. The state has said it is complying with a broader order by Judge I'Ashea L. Myles requiring the preservation of evidence.
But in a Friday court filing, the state asked the judge to rescind the part of her order allowing Pike's legal team to inspect, collect and test any leftover pentobarbital from the execution attempt.
Tennessee Department of Correction fears it will lose its lethal drug supplier

In an affidavit cited in the state's filing, a Tennessee Department of Correction employee said the drug supplier would become identifiable if Pike's legal team is allowed to handle vials of pentobarbital left over from the execution attempt, or review the vials' labeling. The employee, whose name was not disclosed, wrote that residue of the pentobarbital used in Pike's botched execution is "most likely to be found" in vials of the substance used in the attempted execution.

The employee stated the state's supplier was concerned that even with redactions on the labels, the source of the pentobarbital would be identifiable. The employee said that another supplier had stopped communicating with the department in 2024 after its identity was exposed and that the state would likely be unable to find other providers if it lost access to its current source for the drug.

"Pike's counsel and experts cannot be allowed to see, handle, or otherwise get the information on the leftover vials of pentobarbital from Pike's attempted execution," Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti wrote in a court filing.
Tennessee law prohibits the public disclosure of any individual or entity involved in procuring lethal substances or carrying out executions.
The head of Tennessee's Department of Correction resigned in the wake of the failed execution attempt.

In a court filing last month, Pike's attorneys said her veins may have ruptured before she was injected with pentobarbital. The execution team used about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, her lawyers said in the filing.
Pike's attorney says accessing the lethal drug is key
Luke Ihnen, a lawyer representing Pike, said that publicly identifying the state's lethal injection drug supplier "has never been the goal" of the litigation.

He said that it is important for Pike's legal team to be able to review how the pentobarbital used in her botched execution was labeled and stored to understand if there were issues with how it was mixed, transported or handled, and whether it was expired.
"We still don't know exactly what happened that night," Ihnen said. "Those types of things are all valuable pieces of information about what went wrong."
Tennessee Department of Correction spokesperson Dorinda Carter declined to comment, citing pending litigation.
Governor-elect calls for alternative methods of execution

Pike was hospitalized on a ventilator for days following the failed execution. Her attorneys said at the time she had pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow and was unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in a Tennessee hospital. She has returned to prison and said she remains in constant pain.

In a statement she released exactly one month after surviving the botched execution, Pike said she had entered the execution chamber having said her goodbyes and "had not contemplated life beyond that night."

"Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain," she said in a statement dictated to her lawyers. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike and her boyfriend tortured and stabbed a 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to death in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, making her one of the youngest women sentenced to death. Slemmer's mother had traveled from Florida to witness Pike's execution.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike's failed execution. The governor named Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner.

Pike's failed execution has raised questions about Tennessee's lethal injection protocol, marking the state's second execution issue this year. In May, death row inmate Tony Carruthers received a one-year reprieve after officials spent more than an hour unsuccessfully trying to establish an IV line.
CBS News reviewed the state's lethal injection protocols going back to 2007 and found that over the years the protocols grew increasingly vague.

Prior to 2025, the Tennessee lethal injection protocols were laid out in detail over 100 pages and included extensive protocols. But in the most recent version, released to the public early last year, there were only 44 pages to guide members of the execution team through the process.

Tennessee paused its executions in 2022 in order to investigate its lethal injection procedure. It resumed them in 2025, carrying out three of them with a new lethal cocktail that consisted of a single drug, pentobarbital, rather than the combination of three it used formerly.
Pike's attorneys want Republican Gov. Bill Lee, who is set to leave office in January, to change her death sentence to life in prison.

"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," one of Pike's attorneys, Steve Ferrell, told "CBS Mornings" last month.

He has said that she will remain on death row unless a court determines otherwise. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican governor-elect, has called for the state to explore alternative methods of execution, including the electric chair.
The governor has tapped a former U.S. attorney to conduct an independent review of the failed execution, and called off the remaining executions scheduled in Tennessee for the rest of the year.

title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
summary: A U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
story: A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.

The 41-year-old suspect was not identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News he is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He was arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, which is about 100 miles west of London.

The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and they are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.

The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive," although it seems none of the participants expect any immediate breakthroughs, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejecting European demands for an immediate ceasefire.

U.K. police said the arrest was not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations," meaning it appears to be unrelated to the recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, which officials have said is linked to Iran. The U.S. military last month removed its bombers from that base after a security incident that led to the arrests of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national in late September. There are U.S. troops stationed at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at RAF Fairford. One of the suspects is in custody in New York. However, the other two are not in custody at this time, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: Hegseth decries impeachment effort with vote expected tonight
summary: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie said a vote in the House is expected later Tuesday on the impeachment resolutions against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Update: The House on Tuesday night blocked the effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Read earlier developments below.

Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday defiantly denounced the impeachment effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle" ahead of an expected vote in the House on the measure later in the day.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said.
The defense secretary called Massie's impeachment effort an attempt to harm President Trump because of his own "personal animus" for the president and dislike of the Trump administration's policies.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said.
The House is expected to take up the impeachment resolution Tuesday evening, Massie said, but will likely first hold a procedural vote to table the measure.

In his remarks at the Defense Department, Hegseth claimed that the impeachment effort targeting him is only the first step and will next lead to actions against service members who participated in strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," he said. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."
Hegseth likened the attempt to impeach him to Mr. Trump's two impeachments. While the House voted twice to impeach the president during his first term, he was acquitted both times by the Senate.

"If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week," he said. Hegseth said the House never moved to impeach his predecessor, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, who served during the Biden administration.

Hegseth listed the actions the Defense Department has taken so far during Mr. Trump's second term, including launching military operations against Iran, and hailed the president for demonstrating leadership by going to war with Tehran.

The defense secretary said he has a "ton of support" on Capitol Hill and said Republicans "don't want to vote for something that isn't real," echoing his claim that the articles of impeachment are "flimsy."
Shortly after Hegseth finished his remarks, Mr. Trump praised his Pentagon chief and denounced Massie.
"Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" the president wrote on Truth Social.

The briefing comes one day after Massie introduced updated articles of impeachment against Hegseth. The resolution accuses Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations. Under House rules, the chamber has two legislative days to schedule a vote.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has criticized Hegseth for months. But his renewed impeachment push follows Republicans' sweeping defeats in the midterms, which members of both parties blamed on the Iran war and soaring energy prices. The war's status is unclear: Mr. Trump said Monday he plans to maintain the "status quo" and doesn't believe escalating the war will be necessary.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who represents New York, said Monday afternoon he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment resolution, telling reporters Hegseth "abused his power" and is the "architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran."

It remains to be seen whether Republicans other than Massie will vote in favor of the articles of impeachment. Massie said Monday afternoon he did not have a commitment from any other Republicans that they would support it.

Until Democrats take control of the House in January, any impeachment effort would need support from at least three Republicans — if all Democrats vote in favor and depending on any absences. Removing Hegseth from office by convicting him in the Senate is a much heavier lift, requiring more than a dozen Republicans to join the effort.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told CBS News: "impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now … in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look."
The GOP leader told reporters Tuesday that he expects the House will defeat the impeachment push.
"You don't impeach a Cabinet secretary lightly," Johnson said. "They had no due process. There's nothing that went into this. This is just purely for people to get attention, and it's shameful."

Other Republicans have not definitively ruled it out. Rep. French Hill of Arkansas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend, "I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."

Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a moderate who is retiring in January, said Monday he's "wrestling" with the issue, telling reporters, "I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that?"
Asked by reporters about the impeachment bid, Hegseth said Monday, "We're not worried about that."
In a social media video last week, Hegseth criticized Massie, who is leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.
Mr. Trump told reporters Monday he will stand by Hegseth if he's impeached, defending his Pentagon chief and calling Massie a "stone-cold loser."
"What has Hegseth done?" he said. "Pete Hegseth won two wars. 'Oh, let's impeach him.'"

Massie said Monday: "I would like to see him go through the eight articles of impeachment. Just make the argument from a podium. You can use notes. Get the lawyers to help you. Tell us why you are not guilty of each of these eight articles of impeachment."

title: Study shows who is hit hardest by data center costs
summary: A new study found that lower-income, rural households bore a disproportionate share of the financial burdens associated with AI data centers and the energy they use.
story: With data centers cropping up around the United States, the cost of the energy infrastructure on which they rely, and who pays for it, are among the country's most debated economic and political questions. A new study finds that in 2025, the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers landed hardest on lower-income, rural households, which bore disproportionate shares of the financial burdens compared with the data centers themselves.

Authored by Cornell University researchers and published this week in the journal Nature Energy, the study analyzed growth in both energy demand and infrastructure projects along four major U.S. power grids between 2020 and 2025. It also looked at data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers across the U.S. Its results showed that the AI boom, and the buildout of data centers used to support it, hike up energy costs in ways that place the greatest economic strain on people who benefit least from the technology.

The study found that data centers unevenly raised wholesale power prices. Those costs are determined through an open marketplace where electricity is bought and sold in bulk between power generators and utilities before reaching transmission lines, and, eventually, consumers. Power grids that were already stretched saw the greatest price increases, researchers said.

In California's southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to raise wholesale energy prices by almost 20% last year. In Texas' Dallas-Fort Worth area, the increase in 2025 approached 17%, according to their estimates. Both regions have seen influxes of data centers in recent years. Places like New York, where data centers are less prevalent, didn't experience significant changes in wholesale energy prices, according to the study.

Higher wholesale prices had a downstream effect on energy consumers, the researchers said, as residential customers paid huge fractions of the spending on transmission built for data centers. The study found that spending across the four power grids jumped from $2 billion in 2020 to $34.2 billion in 2025, with data centers responsible for $8.25 billion of energy infrastructure costs last year. Residential users were responsible for just under $3.5 billion, but they were billed more than $16 billion while data centers were billed about $3 billion.

Researchers said that antiquated formulas used to allocate energy costs along a power grid have historically divided those costs based on previous energy consumption, rather than new growth. That means households take on much of the costs for developing new power infrastructure.

"It's kind of a chicken-and-egg problem," said Fengqi You, one of the study's authors, in a statement. "Because if you're going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there's no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they're not using energy."

Residents of rural and lower-income areas saw their bills skyrocket, and in some cases faced increases in energy costs that were 76% larger than residents of urban communities, according to the study.

The researchers said that despite the concentration of data centers near metropolitan hubs, the financial loads they trigger often seep into surrounding suburban and rural areas because of policies that govern how energy costs are shared across regions. They argued that such policies warrant review.

Researchers also pointed to what they called a "paradoxical mismatch": According to the study, states that faced the largest cost increases, like West Virginia and Ohio, also reported the lowest uses of generative AI compared with other states around the country.

The study also found instances where states saw price increases linked to AI data centers located geographically far from them, essentially paying for infrastructure "they neither contribute to nor benefit from," researchers said. Residents in New Jersey and Pennsylvania helped pay for power grid updates tied to data center growth in Virginia, for example.

"As I often emphasize, you do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure," You told CBS News. "Our goal is to provide science-based evidence so policymakers, companies, and communities can make informed decisions about how to balance these benefits and costs."

Researchers suggested that data centers cut back on their energy use during their region's peak demand hours or pay states directly for the new energy demand they add to a given power grid. Since regulating data centers was a huge focus of November's midterm elections, You said his team hoped their findings could help lawmakers decide what to do next.

"This is an issue that connects directly to debates in many states and in Congress," said You. "We want to provide science-based evidence and concrete data so that all the stakeholders can better understand the picture and weigh their options."

You told CBS News that, eventually, "the key idea is that the data center sector should really pay for the power energy infrastructure upgrades they need, not the other customers, not the households, and definitely not the low-income ones." But, he added, "unfortunately, that's the situation right now."

title: Sanders won't back Schumer as Democratic leader
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader in the new Congress, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.
story: Washington — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader when the party takes control of the Senate, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.

Sanders made the announcement at a press conference at the Capitol, saying last week's midterm elections were "about change." Democrats will control at least 54 seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

"It was an election across the country, in red states and blue states, where people were looking around them and saying, 'What is going on in America, when I am struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing, and I'm worried not only that my life economically is going nowhere, everything being equal, my kid in the richest country in the history of the world is going to have the lowest standard of living than I do?' And while all of this is going on, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good," Sanders said.

He added: "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, called for "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."
"We need to have that out in the open to show the American people that a new day has come and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington," he said.

Sanders appeared alongside Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said that "whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then in particular how they're going to communicate differently."
Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

No contender has emerged to challenge Schumer's role atop the Senate Democratic caucus, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has come the closest to throwing his hat in the ring. After initially saying he would not pursue the position, Van Hollen has said this week that he's exploring a potential run.
"What I've said from the very beginning is, we shouldn't have a coronation," he said on Monday. "I'm in listening mode and haven't shut the door."
At an event on Tuesday, Van Hollen said he is "in the process right now of calling my colleagues."
"I'm actively calling my colleagues because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus," he said.
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December.

title: 3 Iran-backed operatives indicted for alleged role in terror plots
summary: Three Iran-linked operatives are accused of plotting a terrorist attack at an air base in the U.K. and attempting over a dozen attacks in the U.S. and Europe.
story: Three Iran-backed operatives have been charged with plotting a terrorist attack at a British Royal Air Force base in the United Kingdom where U.S. troops are stationed, the Justice Department announced on Tuesday.

Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi was indicted in May on federal charges of conspiracy to provide material support to Iran-backed terrorist organizations, including Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. He is accused in an eight-count superseding indictment made public Tuesday of attempting to coordinate with two other operatives to attack the British Royal Air Force base in the U.K. in September.

Al-Saadi is currently in federal custody in New York. In Tuesday's filing, the Justice Department alleged that he had plotted the air base attack with Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, by "passing them coded messages through third parties."
Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Federal prosecutors allege that beginning in August, Al-Saadi "directed and paid" associates in the United Kingdom to prepare for and arrange an attack at RAF Fairford, including directing an unnamed individual to conduct surveillance at the air base. Al-Saadi then allegedly later paid multiple unnamed people to organize vans and barrels of fuel, and to research chemical accelerants and buy metal to be used as shrapnel for a potential attack.
The indictment alleges that three individuals would then drive the vans, filled with fuel, to RAF Fairford, where they would explode.

Prosecutors say Al-Saadi told the individuals to mark the vans with custom decals to disguise themselves as a fuel delivery or pool supply business and directed his family members to pass messages to his co-conspirators.

In one phone call with his sister from July, Al-Saadi asked his sister to pass on messages to Mohajeri about "work," referring to terrorist activity, and asked if some of their work was canceled or paused.
Al-Saadi's sister replied that the work "isn't cancelled."
On Sept. 24, Al-Saadi allegedly asked how al-Hassani was, and instructed his family to "give him money so we can do it," referring to the RAF Fairford attack.

The indictment then alleges that al-Hassani directed three individuals to drive the vans on Sept. 26 to RAF Fairford. Two of the vans encountered security checkpoints and were not able to proceed on their intended route to the base, the indictment alleges.
Federal prosecutors said that law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three vans with fuel delivery business decals on them and arrested the drivers.

Prosecutors previously alleged that Al-Saadi had plotted to carry out terror attacks in the U.S., including at a prominent Jewish institution in New York. They also accused him of being "involved in the planning, execution and promotion" of approximately 18 reported terror attacks in Europe and two in Canada against U.S. and Israeli interests since March, in retaliation against the U.S. and Israel's military actions in Iran.
In a statement, Attorney General Todd Blanche said "anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

title: Timeline: The disappearance of Maya Millete
summary: Maya Millete, 39, went missing in January 2021. What was happening between her and her husband before she disappeared and what does spellcasting have to do with it?
story: This article was originally published on Feb. 18, 2022.
Maya Millete, 39, went missing in January 2021. What was happening between her and her husband before she disappeared and what does spellcasting have to do with it?
Mother of three, Maya (May) Millete was 39 when she was last seen on surveillance video arriving at her home in Chula Vista, California.
Maya's husband of 21 years, Larry Millete, was the last person to see Maya. When asked about Maya, he told her family different stories about where she might have gone.

After not hearing from Maya for two days, her sister Maricris Drouaillet    reported her missing to the Chula Vista Police Department. Family and friends made flyers to spread awareness about her disappearance.

Maya's older sister, Maricris and her husband Richard Drouaillet were hoping against hope that Maya was somehow OK, but they say they knew something terrible had really happened when Maya didn't show up for her daughter's birthday.

Attorney Billy Little, a former criminal defense investigator for the U.S. Navy, heard about Maya's disappearance and wanted to help. On January 11, 2021, Little went to the Millete home and looked for clues. He says Larry Millete seemed unconcerned about his wife and it looked like he was airing out the house.

"I love you honey, just come back home," said Larry Millete during a phone interview with local media. "I'm still very hopeful that will (with) all this media coverage, she'll turn up and say, 'Hey, I'm OK.'" On that same day friends, family, and neighbors searched for Maya at Mount San Miguel Park.
The Chula Vista Police Department issued a search warrant at Maya and Larry Millete's home. The goal was to obtain evidence that would lead to finding Maya. Investigators seized some of Larry's guns.

The Chula Vista Police Department and Maya's family held a press conference pleading for help to find Maya. "Please bring her home." Maricris Drouailett cried. "If you have any information, please help us find my sister …"

Since Maya's disappearance, a group called "Help Find Maya" has been out searching for her most weekends. The group has searched areas in Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, Otay Lakes and Marron Valley Road.

Billy Little says he found evidence that Larry Millete purchased spells online. According to Little, Larry first tried spells to get Maya to fall back in love with him. But as the couple's marital problems worsened, police say, Larry eventually wanted to harm her. He later asked a spellcaster, "Please punish May and incapacitate her enough so she can't leave the house. It's time to take the gloves off."

During the investigation by the Chula Vista Police Department, multiple search warrants were served at the Millete home. On May 7,2021, Larry Millete was served with a gun violence restraining order and had to surrender more firearms to authorities.
Nine months after her disappearance, Larry Millete was arrested for the murder of his wife Maya. He has pleaded not guilty and continues to say she willingly left and abandoned the family.

Many dedicated search volunteers like Keri Park have never met Maya. She and others drive for hours to get to the search locations and have spent days looking for Maya. "It's just hard. I mean, you just want closure for this family so much," Park told "48 Hours" contributor Jonathan Vigliotti. "And I just want to bring her home."

After a year without Maya, the Help Find Maya community has created merchandise, held vigils, rallies, and raised more than $50,000 for search efforts. They put QR codes on flyers for people to scan for more information and to recruit volunteers.
In August 2024, a judge granted custody of Maya's three children to her sister, Maricris.
On July 9, 2026, a jury found Larry Millete guilty of first-degree murder in the death of Maya Millete.

On Nov. 2, 2026, Larry Millete was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison for the murder of his wife. He also received a two-year sentence to be served consecutively for a gun charge. Parole was denied.
Maya Millete has never been found.
Anyone with information about Maya's disappearance is asked to contact San Diego County Crime Stoppers at 888-580-8477 or the Chula Vista Police Department at 619-691-5139.

title: House GOP elects Jim Jordan as next leader in major shakeup
summary: Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise for the role of minority leader.
story: Washington — House Republicans voted to elevate Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to lead the party in the next Congress, selecting him over current Majority Leader Steve Scalise following the GOP's crippling losses in last week's midterm elections.

Jordan is a hard-line conservative and close ally of President Trump. His ascension to minority leader represents a significant shakeup for House Republicans, who are looking to rebuild after losing more than 40 House seats.
Tuesday's vote was 106 to 73, sources familiar with the tally told CBS News.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom. And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day," Jordan said in brief remarks after the leadership elections.
House Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping down from leadership and has been noncommittal in recent days about his long-term future in Congress.

Jordan and Scalise both ran for House speaker after Kevin McCarthy's ouster in 2023, leading to weeks of turbulence in the House. But Jordan and Scalise failed to unite the party's various factions. Johnson — who was then a little-known conservative with no leadership experience — pulled off a surprise victory with the conference voting unanimously to make him speaker.
Jordan helped start the conservative House Freedom Caucus and has chaired the House Judiciary Committee since 2023.

"For too long, we have operated without a clear plan to survive the hour or the day in front of us. That will not cut it against an emboldened and energetic Democratic majority," Jordan said in his candidacy letter, arguing that he was "battle-tested."
Scalise, a Louisiana Republican, has held leadership roles since 2014, serving as majority and minority whip before becoming majority leader in 2023.

Scalise was critically injured when a gunman opened fire on a congressional baseball practice in 2017. In 2023, Scalise announced he had been diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He said several months later that he was in remission after undergoing treatment.
"This is no doubt a challenging time for our conference, but overcoming adversity is nothing new to me," Scalise said in his letter to his Republican colleagues announcing his candidacy.

Rounding out the rest of the GOP leadership team is Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota as minority whip, Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan as conference chair and Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia as chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee.
Emmer and McClain hold the same roles in the majority. Jack will replace Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina as chair of the House GOP's campaign arm. Hudson lost his race for reelection.

title: Thune wins reelection as Senate GOP leader after midterms losses
summary: Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after their brutal midterm losses.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune as their leader on Tuesday, staying the course as they prepare to enter the minority after the party's brutal midterm losses, which saw at least seven Senate seats fall to the Democrats.
Senate Republicans backed Thune for another two years as leader by acclamation, or without opposition, after meeting behind closed doors in the Old Senate Chamber for much of the day.

Thune, 65, is a South Dakota Republican who was first elected leader after the 2024 elections. He's been in the Senate since 2005 and took the helm two decades later, after working under Sen. Mitch McConnell as the No. 2 Senate Republican.
Well-liked by his conference, there was little doubt that Thune would remain leader. But a last-minute push by several conservative members to delay the elections added a wrinkle.

GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin led the push to delay the vote after the disastrous midterm results for Republicans. He secured signatures from a handful of his colleagues — Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah — to compel a conference meeting ahead of Tuesday's elections. But the effort to delay any further fell short.
Johnson told reporters that Senate Republicans "just can't continue on business as usual" after a "stunning defeat" at the polls.
"I mean, that kind of defeat demands change," Johnson said, when asked whether new leadership was needed.
But Johnson conceded that there wasn't a clear alternative to Thune. He argued that Senate Republicans at least needed to hear from their leadership team about the strategy moving forward.
After meeting behind closed doors for two hours Tuesday morning, and reconvening later in the afternoon, Johnson told reporters that "this has never been anything against John Thune."
"I think he has been very unfairly attacked by our base," Johnson said.
For his part, Thune appeared sympathetic to the efforts to regroup, and he acknowledged that the decision over whether to delay selecting their leaders would ultimately come down to members.

"I think in the end, I think it's important that for purposes of moving forward, that we get some of these issues settled as soon as possible," Thune told CBS News on Monday. "We'll see what our members think tomorrow."

Thune's reelection as leader comes after he led Senate Republicans as they passed the president's massive tax, border security and defense agenda, swiftly confirmed the president's nominees, and approved a handful of bipartisan priorities over the last two years. At the same time, his tenure was marked by two record-breaking government shutdowns, and a White House that often moved out of step with Republicans in Congress.

Some Republicans were critical of Thune's record, arguing that the GOP agenda wasn't aggressive enough. Conservative frustrations came to a head over the SAVE America Act, a controversial election bill that President Trump repeatedly pushed. Thune made clear that the legislation did not enjoy enough support in the upper chamber to move forward.

Ahead of the election, Thune pushed back on the criticism about the Senate GOP agenda, telling CBS News, "I don't know how you could be more aggressive." And he defended Senate Republicans' record, while acknowledging that there were factors beyond their control.

Senate Republicans had entered the midterm cycle with a map that initially looked favorable, offering few pickup opportunities for Democrats. But GOP candidates across the country were routed as cost of living concerns and the war in Iran took center stage, and expanded the map for Democrats. The Senate GOP lost seats in battleground states like Ohio and North Carolina, along with Republican strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas and Texas. Two Senate contests — Alaska and Mississippi — remain unresolved, and could yield more victories for Democrats.

Thune, in his first floor speech since the midterms, said, "There is no doubt about it, Tuesday night was a tough election night." He said the election results gave Senate Republicans "an opportunity to reflect on what we as a party need to do better" and "a clear message that this coming Congress needs to double down on the work that we've been doing on affordability."

title: Key moments from ex-cop's trial in the death of Sandra Birchmore
summary: A jury in Massachusetts convicted former police officer Matthew Farwell in the 2021 death of 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore.
story: A jury in Massachusetts convicted Matthew Farwell on Tuesday in his trial over the death of Sandra Birchmore. Federal prosecutors alleged Farwell, a former police officer, killed Birchmore after years of sexual abuse that started when she was a teenager.
Farwell had pleaded not guilty to killing the 23-year-old and her unborn son in 2021. Prosecutors accused Farwell of staging Birchmore's death to look like a suicide.

Prosecutors said Farwell started sexually abusing Birchmore when she was 15 and he was 27. The two met through a police youth program that's designed to teach children about law enforcement careers. Farwell, who worked for the police department in Stoughton, Massachusetts, was an instructor for the program.

Birchmore's manner of death was initially determined by local authorities to be a suicide, but was later changed to undetermined. After a federal investigation into her death, Farwell was charged in 2024 with killing a witness or a victim, with prosecutors alleging that Farwell killed Birchmore to silence her about the abuse. In 2025, he was charged with causing the death of an unborn child.
Farwell didn't take the witness stand during the trial. Attorneys gave their closing arguments on Friday before the case went to the jury.

During the trial in U.S. District Court in Boston, Farwell's attorneys didn't deny that he had an affair with Birchmore. His lawyers instead tried to cast doubt on prosecutors' theory of the case and how she died.
Here are some key takeaways from the trial:
Birchmore wanted a baby from Farwell

When Birchmore learned Farwell was expecting a third child with his wife, Birchmore said she wanted him to impregnate her or else she would tell his wife about the affair, according to text messages revealed during the trial.
"I gave him an ultimatum and I'm getting his baby. He was not at all happy about it," Birchmore said in a text message to a friend in October 2020.
By late December, she was pregnant. On Dec. 28, 2020, she sent Farwell a picture of a poster that said, "Congrats we are goin' to be parents!"
When Birchmore told Farwell he needed to be with her while she's in labor, he responded, "You are truly the worst person on the face of the earth."
The next day, Farwell texted Birchmore, "You extorted me to get what you wanted."
Prosecutors said they met up, and things didn't appear to go well.
"I'm not going to be around anymore and neither is your kid. Congrats. Hope you're happy," Birchmore texted Farwell.
She also told Farwell she felt scared when he was next to her during that meetup. "I thought you were going to hit me," she said.
Prosecution and defense experts disagree on Birchmore's death

Birchmore's body was discovered Feb. 4, 2021, when police conducted a welfare check at her apartment after she didn't show up to work . She was found hanging in a seated position from a door handle by a duffle bag strap.

Prosecutors argued that Farwell used the strap to strangle her and then staged the scene to look like a suicide. Farwell's attorneys, however, noted that Birchmore had written an apparent suicide note in a journal in 2017 and searched on the internet, "What color is the suicide ribbon," days before she was found dead.

A strangulation expert for the prosecution, Dr. William Smock, told jurors that Birchmore's death was a homicide. He said a clasp on the strap caused an injury on her chest and was hanging from the knob, suggesting that the scene was staged. He also said the fracture of Birchmore's hyoid bone, located in the neck, rarely happens in suicides.

Defense expert Heather Garvin, an anthropologist who has a doctorate in anatomy, said the fracture doesn't definitively prove that Birchmore's death was a homicide. Another defense witness, forensic scientist Alicia McCarthy, testified that she couldn't conclude with certainty that the injury on Birchmore's chest was caused by the clasp.

Dr. Thomas Andrew, a former chief medical examiner for the state of New Hampshire who testified for the defense, said that all of the factors of Birchmore's death made him think it was a suicide. "This is not manual strangulation," he said.
Farwell wasn't the father of Birchmore's child

DNA testing found that Farwell didn't father Birchmore's child, FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch testified. Instead, the father was Jason Pickard, a defense contractor for the Air Force who met Birchmore when he was a recruiter for the Army Reserve.
Birchmore, who was 22 at the time, was considering enlisting when she and Pickard, who was married at the time, started texting in December 2019. The relationship eventually became sexual.
When Pickard found out about Birchmore's relationship with Farwell, he said he urged her to report him, but she didn't. He also didn't alert authorities about the relationship.

"I was afraid. I was a married man. I was a recruiter and she was a recruit. I knew what it would do to my marriage, I knew what it would do to my children, I knew what it would do to my career," he said. "I also respected her request not to tell."
When Birchmore became pregnant, she told Pickard the child wasn't his.
Witness says Farwell got upset by call about relationship

On Jan. 20, 2021, about two weeks before Birchmore was found dead, Stoughton police dispatcher James Fitton received a call from a female who "alluded to a relationship between Matthew Farwell and her friend," Fitton said during his testimony.
When Fitton told Farwell about the call, he got angry. "He got visibly and audibly upset with me," Fitton said.
He threw out the note he took about the call after he said his supervisor told him to forget about it.
When Farwell texted Birchmore about the call, she told him the friend owed her money.
Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment before she died

Matthew Dunne, a Massachusetts State Police trooper who initially investigated Birchmore's death, testified that after he learned of the relationship between Birchmore and Farwell, he interviewed Farwell on Feb. 6, 2021.
According to Dunne, Farwell went to Birchmore's apartment on Feb. 1, 2021, which was the last day she was at work.
"The account he provided was that he went over there to break up with her," Dunne said.
Farwell also told Dunne he went to see Birchmore to tell her that the baby wasn't his.
Farwell left Birchmore's apartment building after her phone stopped moving
Dunne confirmed that before Farwell left her apartment, data from Birchmore's phone showed it had stopped moving.
An FBI digital forensic examiner, Christopher Beckstrom, told jurors Birchmore's phone locked for the last time at 9:13 p.m. on Feb. 1, 2021.

Farwell was seen on surveillance video footage entering Birchmore's apartment building that night wearing a hooded sweatshirt and face mask at 9:14 p.m. Birchmore texted Farwell to let him know her door was open, Beckstrom said.
Birchmore's phone recorded eight steps were taken at 9:40 p.m., and no other steps were recorded after that time.
At 9:43 p.m., Farwell was seen on the security camera leaving Birchmore's building. Kelsch testified that Birchmore usually sent Farwell a text after he visited her, but she didn't that night.
Birchmore was excited to be pregnant

Birchmore worked for the school district in the nearby town of Sharon, Massachusetts. She was excited when she learned she was pregnant, according to testimony from Cheryl Carlson, an assistant principal who worked with Birchmore.
Birchmore told Carlson she wanted the baby "to have someone to love."
Birchmore also opened up to Carlson about the baby's father.
"She said that the father was in a committed relationship and that there were children involved, and that the plan was that he was going to leave his situation when her child was born," Carlson said.
She also testified that Birchmore had told third graders that the father was her police officer boyfriend.
Carlson was caught off guard when she learned Birchmore's death was initially called a suicide.
"Suicide didn't make sense to me," she said. "Because she was so excited to have that baby, she was so determined to have the baby, it didn't fit with her character."
Farwell told state police his relationship with Birchmore started much later

Farwell provided Dunne with a different account of his relationship with Birchmore than what prosecutors said. According to Dunne, Farwell said the relationship had been going on for about two to three years, which would have made Birchmore 20 or 21 at the time they began seeing each other.
"I believe he said he was intoxicated at some point and they encountered each other," Dunne said.

But that account conflicts with text messages between Birchmore and Farwell that were read during the trial about how their sexual relationship started when she was 15. When prosecutors asked Dunne if Farwell's contradictory statements were factors in the investigation, Dunne said they were given weight.
"All of this has to be taken into context with the full investigation, but they were definitely given weight," Dunne said.
State police didn't take notes during initial Farwell interviews

Dunne's first interview with Farwell in the school parking lot wasn't recorded and he didn't take any notes. During the trial, he testified that was a tactical decision so Farwell would talk to investigators.
When Dunne and his supervisor, Sgt. John Fanning, who knew Farwell, interviewed him a few days later, neither of them took notes, Dunne testified.

title: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts
summary: More U.S. households are falling into debt as they grapple with medical bills, student loans and other expenses, data show.
story: More Americans are tumbling seriously into debt as prices and the overall cost of living continue to rise.

Roughly 24% of people with a credit record are behind on medical bills, student debt, or auto or retail loans, according to a new analysis from the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The median balance owed: $2,913. In communities of color, 30% of people are behind on payments, with a median debt in collection of $3,009.

"The increasing cost of living makes it harder for people to make payments on basic needs," Breno Braga, senior fellow in the family and financial well-being division at the Urban Institute, told CBS News.

Rising interest rates this year as the Federal Reserve tries to tame inflation are also making it harder for people to catch up. "It's a reflection of the financial life of Americans these days as we know it," Braga added.
Consumers' credit card balances have surged to a record $1.29 trillion, up nearly 70% from five years ago, according to new figures from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Years of high prices have forced Americans to deplete their savings and finance their daily expenses with debt, according to Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit debt counselor. As a result, many household budgets are at a "breaking point," he said in an email to CBS News.

Consumer prices have risen by an average of 30% since 2019, Rossman noted. Meanwhile, the share of Americans with debt in collection this year is up about one percentage point, from less than 23% in 2025, according to the Urban Institute, which based its findings on an analysis of more than 10 million credit records and U.S. Census data.
Student loans and medical bills

Roughly one in six, or almost 16%, of student loan borrowers are behind on payments, although the figure varies by geography. In Louisiana, for example, the state with the highest share of people with debt in collections, the student loan delinquency rate is roughly 22%.
Braga attributes the disparity to several factors, such as lower incomes and higher poverty rates in some parts of the country.

"People there tend to have lower credit scores, so when they get a credit card or take out an auto loan, they tend to pay higher interest rates," he said. "That makes it harder to make those payments, especially if you are low income. It makes you more likely to fall behind."
Many people also are shouldering heavy medical bills despite having health insurance, reflecting insufficient coverage and the high cost of care across the U.S.

According to the Urban Institute, 3% of Americans have medical debt in collections, with a median balance of $1,492 — a figure that reflects only unpaid hospital or other medical bills, while excluding credit card debt stemming from health care costs.

"People without health insurance are more likely to have medical debt, but having coverage does not protect you at all from having medical debt, especially not now with the high deductible plans we are seeing," Braga said.
Fifteen states have passed legislation barring health care providers from reporting medical debt to credit rating agencies, which can lessen the damage to consumers' credit records.
"It's good for patients that it's not reported to the agencies, but that doesn't mean it disappears. It just isn't reported anymore," he noted.

title: FDA warns of rare vision-loss side effect from GLP-1 drugs
summary: The Food and Drug Administration is adding a new warning about possible rare cases of vision loss reported with GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy and other brands.
story: Popular weight loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic and Wegovy, will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday.

The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.

The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.

FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy.

Dr. Joseph Rizzo, a neuro-ophthalmologist at Massachusetts Eye and Ear who co-authored that paper, told CBS News on Monday that he and his team had been working with the FDA to gather and review data on the issue for some time and that, while he didn't know the agency was ready to make a decision, he wasn't surprised it chose to add the warning.

He stressed that while he believes the evidence shows GLP-1 usage increases the risk of developing NAION, he doesn't discourage patients from taking them, saying, "The medicines have really been profoundly beneficial to a large number of people."
People who aren't on GLP-1s can also develop NAION, which affects somewhere between 2 to 10 of every 100,000 adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology.

Novo Nordisk, the maker of Wegovy and Ozempic, said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines."

"We recognize that NAION can have a profound impact on patients and their families," it said. "Patient safety is a top priority for Novo, and we continue to monitor the safety of our medicines, review new research and work with health authorities around the world."
Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound and Mounjaro, said in a statement Monday it was "carefully evaluating the update and will respond to FDA promptly."

"Patient safety is Lilly's top priority," the company said. "FDA's drug safety communication applies to all medicines with GLP-1 RA activity and does not reference any findings specific to Lilly medicines."

An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.

Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a healthcare professional immediately, the agency said.
Rizzo noted that the vision loss from the condition tends to be irreversible and can become progressively worse, even if a patient stops taking the medication.

"Usually when you lose vision, although there may be some mild degree of improvement, it's usually not a large degree of improvement," he said. "And unfortunately, a great frustration for so many of our patients and doctors who take care of patients with NAION  is the fact that we do not really know how to mitigate the risk."
Rizzo also said the condition does not necessarily affect each eye the same.

"The degree of visual loss in the first eye does not inform the degree of visual loss that would occur in the second eye," he told CBS News. "So you could have mild visual loss in one eye, and then the next eye could be severe."
