Trump also said he did not think he would raise the matter with Xi.
The White House declined to elaborate on whether the Trump administration would continue engaging with Huang, referring Fox News Digital to Trump’s previous comments.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump signals surprising approach to choosing his successor as GOP's 2028 field grows
summary: Trump says he may not endorse in the 2028 Republican Party presidential primary
story: Vance or Rubio? MAGA voters speaking with Fox News Digital ahead of a recent Trump rally reveal their early picks for 2028 Republican presidential nomination
President Donald Trump says he may not put his thumb on the scale when it comes to picking the Republican Party's 2028 presidential nominee.

"Probably, not necessarily," Trump said in a post-midterm election interview on CBS' "60 Minutes" when asked whether he will endorse in the primary to pick the next Republican nominee. "So I may or may not get involved... Maybe I'm better off not getting involved."
Trump for months has touted the GOP's "great bench" when asked about the likely Republican field of contenders aiming to succeed him in the White House.
The president reiterated that opinion after the GOP's drubbing in last week's midterm elections, as the party lost control of both the House and the Senate.
VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS
President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. (Getty Images)

"I think we have an unbelievable bench of talent," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum in an election night interview on Fox News.. "We have a great group of talented people that I think would do a very good job."

Early jockeying by the potential contenders began the morning after Election Day, with midterm post-mortems by Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis grabbing plenty of headlines.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"There's going to be a robust field of candidates that test the waters in Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina and that's exactly as it should be," Nicole Schlinger, a veteran Iowa-based Republican strategist, told Fox News Digital. "We're going to get an opportunity to see which approach to our message of where we as the Republican Party goes next is going to resonate the most with the grassroots voters who are going to show up and kick tires."

Here's a look at the list of potential GOP presidential contenders in the burgeoning race to become the party's next standard-bearer and impact which direction the party will head in a post-Trump era.
Vice President JD Vance
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport, Nov. 2, 2026, in Rome, N.Y. (Tom Brenner/Pool Photo via AP)
The vice president has long been viewed as the likely frontrunner for the 2028 GOP nomination and Trump's heir apparent.

But the conventional wisdom from pundits is that the shellacking the GOP took in the midterms has transformed what may have been a Vance coronation into a more competitive and crowded nomination battle.

Vance kicked off the post-midterms debate last Wednesday morning with a roughly 600-word postmortem on X, blaming the war with Iran for the ballot box setbacks, in what some pundits viewed as an early pitch to eventually claim the MAGA and America First mantle.

Even with last week's setbacks, Vance leads many of the early 2028 GOP presidential primary polls, has built a formidable fundraising network thanks in part to his role as the Republican National Committee's finance chair, and has a team of advisors and aides that would form the beginnings of a presidential campaign.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio
Secretary of State Marco Rubio attends a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 7. (Yves Herman/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Rubio, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination, is doing his best to stay far away from the 2028 spotlight.

The former senator from Florida has long been floated by Trump and by pundits as a possible White House contender, and his support in early 2028 polls has soared. But Rubio has downplayed such speculation, and dismissed reports he was considering stepping down as secretary of state to lay the groundwork for a presidential run.

Rubio, who has said a handful of times over the past year that he'd back Vance if the vice president decides to launch a White House campaign, was asked about 2028 Monday while taking questions from reporters during a stop in France.
"I don't know why you're wasting your time," Rubio said. "I'm not going to talk about 2028 any longer. I'm just not going to talk about 2028 anymore."
Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks during a campaign rally with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Grosse Point Woods, Mich., Oct. 28, 2026. (Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images)
The conservative firebrand senator from Texas, who was runner-up to Trump in the bruising 2016 presidential primaries, has made no secret that he may run for the White House again in 2028.
In his post-Election Day assessment, Cruz described the midterms as a "blue tsunami" and warned that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State.
"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."
In a possible preview of the Republican primaries, Cruz has put plenty of daylight between himself and Vance over support for Israel, with Cruz spotlighting his support for the Israeli government.
Boosting Cruz if he decides to run would be his top-ranked podcast, "Verdict with Ted Cruz," which has allowed the senator to build a massive grassroots network.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis
Gov. Ron DeSantis holds a press conference at the State Emergency Operations Center regarding Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 8, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters)

The term-limited conservative Florida governor, who finishes up in Tallahassee at the start of the new year, ran for the White House in 2024. He was an early frontrunner before being decisively defeated by Trump.
DeSantis held a news conference the morning after Election Day when he called the midterm election results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country."

"Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt — not just for the next two years... That is something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he said. "We knew it could be worse. I don't think most of us thought it would be this bad."

But DeSantis, who sat for a slew of media interviews in the wake of the midterms, repeatedly highlighted that "the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida."

While 2028 buzz about DeSantis surged since last week's election, the governor took to social media on Friday to blast a report that he was planning a 2028 run, emphasizing, "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything. Just another pathetic attempt to garner clicks."
Former Vice President Mike Pence
Former Vice President Mike Pence is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on March 18, 2026, in Washington D.C. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Pence, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, has said he has "no plans" to run for the White House again in 2028.
But Pence has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year.

And Trump's first vice president told Fox News Digital earlier this year that his fight to keep the Republican Party from drifting too far from its conservative roots and principles, amid a rise of populism in the GOP and big government creep during Trump's second administration, is "the calling of my life right now."

Last week Pence argued, "The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism, and our majorities in Congress and state legislatures and governorships across the country paid the price."
But he emphasized, "The conservative comeback starts today."
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp
Term-limited GOP Gov. Brian Kemp, right, endorses Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the Republican gubernatorial runoff, in Atlanta, Georgia, on June 15, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
The conservative term-limited governor, who finishes out his tenure in Atlanta in two months, is also seen as a potential White House contender.
In the wake of the midterm shellacking, Kemp spelled out a GOP vision centered on the "conservative principles of our party."
"It’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come," the governor wrote.
Former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin

Former GOP Gov. Glenn Youngkin of Virginia, left, teams up on the campaign trail on the eve of the Wisconsin primary with Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, on Aug. 10, 2026, in Oconomowoc, Wisconsin. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Youngkin, who instantly soared to political stardom after his 2021 gubernatorial victory energized Republicans a year after Trump lost the White House and the Senate in the 2020 election, has consistently downplayed talk of a 2028 presidential campaign.
Instead, Youngkin has focused on his signature issue  — education  — by pushing to promote school choice programs through his recently formed national policy group Empowering America's Parents.
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, a 2024 Republican presidential candidate, is interviewed on the campaign trail by Fox News Digital. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Christie, who unsuccessfully ran for the 2016 and 2024 GOP nominations, is seriously mulling a third run for the White House.

"The midterms were a repudiation of the GOP and Donald Trump. It is time Republicans do the autopsy, learn the lessons and move forward," Christie, a vocal Republican critic of the president, argued in the days after last week's election. "The Trump era is over. He has led us to the greatest losses this country has seen for a party since Richard Nixon."
Christie has said he'll decide on a presidential run in the next few months, telling Fox News Digital recently, "I think there’s a lot of flexibility on the timing."
Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., arrives at a House Republican Conference meeting in the U.S. Capitol Building on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Bacon, a former Air Force brigadier general who has at times split with Trump on foreign policy and national security issues, decided against running for re-election this year and exits Congress in two months.
Bacon has said he is open to a potential run for president in 2028 or serving in a supporting role on another Republican candidate's ticket.
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders participates in the first National Outdoor Recreation Executive Forum on May 7, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Outdoor Recreation Roundtable)
Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as Trump’s White House press secretary for much of his first term.
Sanders, who made history four years ago as the first woman elected Arkansas governor and last week won re-election by double digits, is increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender.
Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas

Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas joins GOP colleagues in speaking to reporters following Senate Republican policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 23, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Cotton, who took a hard look at a 2024 GOP presidential run before deciding against launching a campaign, was just re-elected.

The senator, an Army veteran who served in combat in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars before becoming a rising star in the Republican Party and who was on Trump's running mate short list two years ago, is also viewed as a potential White House hopeful.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida
Republican Sen. Rick Scott is interviewed by Fox News Digital on March 6, 2026, in Palm Beach, Florida. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
Scott, a self-made multimillionaire and former two-term governor who's the wealthiest member of the Senate, also mulled a 2024 bid before running for re-election.

Midterm election campaign trail stops in Iowa and New Hampshire  — the two states that lead off the Republican presidential nominating calendar  — sparked speculation that Scott was considering a 2028 campaign.
Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., speaks to members of the media at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kennedy, who's up for re-election in 2028, has said he would consider a White House run instead of seeking another term in the Senate if he felt he could no longer be effective in the Senate or if he felt dissatisfied with the Republican presidential primary field.
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo
Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo (Siavosh Hosseini/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Pompeo, a former four-term congressman from Kansas who served as CIA director and later as the top U.S. diplomat in Trump's first administration, also took a hard look at a 2024 run before passing.
Asked last year about a 2028 bid, Pompeo told Fox News Digital, "We'll see what the good Lord brings in a couple of years."
He's currently viewed by pundits as a possible contender.
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie is interviewed by Fox News Digital, on May 18, 2026, in Mason County, Kentucky (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

The vocal Republican critic of the president who relentlessly pressed for the release of the Epstein files before losing his bid for renomination earlier this year to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein has said he's "not ruling anything in or out" when it comes to a presidential bid.

Last week, Axios first reported that a group of Libertarian Party operatives and anti-Trump MAGA defectors was urging Massie to run for the White House as a third-party or Libertarian presidential candidate.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Is AI deciding who's dangerous in Michigan prisons?
summary: Michigan's new prison scoring system claims 30% better violence prediction, but Recidiviz says it doesn't actually use AI to classify inmates.
story: Incarcerated men participate in employment counseling at a Michigan prison, where security classifications can affect access to job training and educational opportunities. (Michigan Department of Corrections)

What if a computer-generated score could influence whether someone lives in a low-security prison dorm or a tightly controlled cell? Michigan is preparing to test new technology that could affect exactly that.

State officials say the system could improve predictions of future prison violence by approximately 30%. That's a big claim, especially when the safety of correctional officers and incarcerated people could depend on getting those assessments right.

But there's something important missing from early reports about Michigan prison AI. Despite headlines suggesting artificial intelligence will determine how dangerous someone might be, the nonprofit developing the software says AI plays no role in calculating security scores.

Instead, the technology follows predetermined rules, and corrections staff make the final decisions. So, how does the system work? And can Michigan really predict prison violence more accurately without putting too much trust in a computer-generated score?
FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH

Why security levels can change life behind bars

The Michigan Department of Corrections oversees approximately 32,000 incarcerated people statewide. Currently, corrections employees use a manual scoring process to determine the appropriate security level for each person. Those classifications influence where someone lives and how closely they're supervised. They can also affect access to educational programs and job training opportunities. For someone serving a lengthy sentence, a change in security level can make a significant difference in daily life.

Michigan has four general population security levels: I, II, IV and V. Level I generally allows greater freedom of movement, while Level V involves much tighter supervision. People at lower security levels may have access to more vocational training and higher education opportunities. However, Michigan says programs such as Violence Prevention Programming remain available at every general population security level. There is no general population Level III. Now, the state wants a better way to determine which security level fits each person's current behavior and needs.
What Michigan's new scoring system will change

The Michigan Department of Corrections plans to begin testing the new system on Dec. 1 at selected men's prisons. If the pilot performs well, officials could eventually expand the technology to additional facilities. One significant change involves how often corrections staff can reassess someone's security level. Instead of relying on information collected at scheduled intervals, the new system will allow ongoing reviews using updated prison records. That could help staff recognize changes in behavior sooner.

The software comes from Recidiviz, a nonprofit technology organization that supports criminal justice agencies in 19 states. Its team analyzed 10 years of Michigan prison classification data to help redesign the state's scoring process. Here's how it works. The software examines information already in prison records and calculates a score using factors selected by Michigan corrections experts. Recent disciplinary incidents may carry more weight than incidents from years ago. Meanwhile, someone who maintains good behavior over time may have an opportunity to qualify for a lower security level.

Completing certain rehabilitation programs can also help someone qualify for a less restrictive classification. Additionally, the software can flag a person's record when new information warrants another review. Michigan Department of Corrections Director Heidi E. Washington believes the changes could help improve safety.

"Classifying prisoners at the security level that fits their current behaviors and needs keeps everyone safer," Washington said in the state's announcement. She also expressed optimism that the combination of historical information and research-based scoring could strengthen security throughout Michigan's prison system. The idea sounds promising. But how much confidence should officials place in those computer-generated scores?
GRANDMOTHER SUES AFTER ALLEGED AI FACIAL RECOGNITION ERROR LED TO MONTHS IN JAIL, EXPERTS SOUND ALARM
Michigan uses four general population security levels, from Level I with the fewest restrictions to Level V with the tightest supervision. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
Is Michigan actually using AI to predict prison violence?

This is where the story takes an unexpected turn. On Nov. 2, Recidiviz published an explanation titled, Why We Don't Use AI to Classify People in Prisons. The nonprofit confirmed that Michigan's new classification system does not use artificial intelligence to calculate security scores. The system relies on a points-based formula that corrections employees can examine.

You may hear this type of formula called an algorithm. That's simply a set of instructions a computer follows to complete a task. Think of it like a digital scorecard. The computer reviews specific information and adds up the points according to established rules. Give it the same information, and it produces the same score.

Recidiviz says Michigan corrections experts helped determine which factors belong in the scoring process. Staff can review the calculations and override a score when circumstances require it. For example, someone might have medical needs or personal safety concerns that call for a different housing assignment. Corrections employees can consider that information before making the final decision.

Now, Recidiviz does use AI in other parts of its technology platform. Some tools help corrections employees prepare case notes and organize information from meetings. However, the organization says AI does not determine someone's security level or release. And here's what I find interesting. We're hearing about AI being used in nearly every industry. Yet this particular system relies on a more traditional approach to computer software.

That clarification is important because people deserve to understand how technology influences decisions affecting someone's daily life. Still, using a rules-based system doesn't guarantee perfect results. Even straightforward software can produce questionable scores when the information behind its calculations contains errors.
Can Michigan really predict prison violence 30% better?

This is the number that really caught my attention. In its Oct. 28 announcement, the Michigan Department of Corrections said the redesigned system is expected to improve its ability to predict future violence by approximately 30%. That's a substantial improvement if the technology delivers it. However, the announcement doesn't explain how officials calculated that figure or provide the underlying performance results.

For example, will the system identify more people who might become violent? Could it also incorrectly classify someone as dangerous? And how will officials know whether it's performing better than the current process? Those questions deserve answers because someone's security classification can affect their daily life throughout their sentence.

There's another issue worth considering. The software depends on prison records. If a disciplinary report contains inaccurate information, that mistake could influence someone's score. Even when the information is correct, a risk assessment cannot predict with certainty what someone will do in the future.
NORTHEASTERN CITY VOTES TO END SHOTSPOTTER CONTRACT FOR GUNFIRE-DETECTION TECH DESIGNED TO FIGHT CRIME

An MDOC employment counselor reaches for materials inside a Michigan correctional facility's resource center, where educational and employment resources help incarcerated individuals prepare for life after prison. (Michigan Department of Corrections)
Why better prison technology may not solve Michigan's biggest problem

Even if Michigan's new software delivers more accurate security scores, officials still face a challenge that technology cannot solve on its own. What happens when someone needs higher-security housing but there's no appropriate bed available? Byron Osborn, president of the union representing Michigan corrections officers, raised that concern in recent reporting.

According to Osborn, the department faces a shortage of higher-security beds. He argues that the bigger problem involves a lack of appropriate housing for people already classified as higher risk. Consider what happens if the software identifies someone who needs tighter supervision. Corrections staff agree with the assessment, but the prison lacks space in the appropriate security unit.

Now what? The computer may have helped identify a potential safety concern. However, officials still need somewhere appropriate to house that person. Michigan has announced plans to add 870 high-security beds as part of its Safe Prisons Initiative. Some facility conversions are already underway, while larger construction projects will take longer to complete.

More than 400 of those beds will come from two new high-security units at Oaks Correctional Facility and St. Louis Correctional Facility. The state expects those construction projects to take approximately two and a half years. Osborn has warned that corrections officers and incarcerated people need solutions sooner.

Meanwhile, the state has experienced serious violence inside its prisons, including several recent incidents in which incarcerated people were suspected of killing their cellmates. Better classification could help officials recognize potentially dangerous situations sooner. But the department still needs sufficient staffing and appropriate housing to respond. And that raises another question. How much safer can a prison become if officials identify a problem but lack the resources to address it?
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why Michigan wants to try something new. Nobody wants to see more violence inside prisons, and if technology can help prevent it, I'm all for giving it a chance. But I was surprised to learn that despite all the talk about AI, this new system actually uses a fairly straightforward scoring process. Corrections staff still make the final decisions, which I think is important when you're dealing with people's safety.

Now, that 30% improvement Michigan is talking about sounds impressive. But I'd really like to know how they arrived at that number. And what happens when the computer gets someone's risk level wrong? Maybe a person has turned their life around, but an old disciplinary record still works against them. That's the kind of situation I'd want someone to take a closer look at before making a decision.

There's also the bigger issue of whether Michigan has enough high-security beds and corrections officers to act on these assessments. You can have the best scoring system in the world, but what good does it do if there's nowhere appropriate to house someone who needs closer supervision? I'll be interested to see what happens when the pilot begins Dec. 1. If it leads to safer prisons and gives people a fairer way to demonstrate they've changed, that would be something worth talking about. But Michigan needs to show us the results.

Would you trust a computer-generated score to help determine how dangerous someone might be, or should decisions affecting someone's safety remain entirely in human hands? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI phishing scams turn your social posts against you
summary: University of Texas at Arlington researchers reveal how AI analyzes public Instagram posts to craft spear phishing emails that feel personal.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the 'CyberGuy', weighs in on warnings of rising AI cyber threats after Bill Gates sounds the alarm. Gates warns of negative surprises within a year and cautions that the world is not prepared for AI upheavals.

You post a few photos from a concert on Instagram. The next day, an email arrives that appears to be from the venue, offering you access to exclusive photos from the show. It mentions the artist you saw and even references the night you attended. Sounds legitimate, right? You might be tempted to click without giving it a second thought. But what if that email came from a scammer who used artificial intelligence to study your social media posts?

That's the alarming possibility researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington have uncovered. Their study shows how widely available AI tools can gather personal details from public social media accounts and turn them into highly convincing phishing emails. Even more concerning, the technology can generate these personalized messages at a scale that once required far more time and effort. Think about the photos and updates you've shared recently. Could someone use those details to convince you an email is legitimate? According to this research, the answer could be yes.

AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
Public social media profiles can reveal personal details that scammers use to create convincing AI-generated phishing emails. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
How AI phishing scams use your social media posts

You've probably seen your share of phishing emails. Maybe someone claims there's a problem with your bank account or a package couldn't be delivered. Many of these scams follow familiar patterns, and we've become pretty good at spotting the obvious ones. But AI is giving scammers a much more personal approach. Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington studied a technique known as context-aware spear phishing. In plain English, it means using details about someone's everyday life to create a scam that feels like it was written specifically for them.

Let's say you recently returned from a vacation in Brazil. You posted photos of the hotel and tagged a few places you visited. A scammer could use AI to analyze those posts and generate an email that appears to come from your hotel. The message might thank you for staying and offer a discount on your next visit. Everything seems to line up with your actual trip. However, the link could lead to a fake website designed to steal your password or credit card information.

Shirin Nilizadeh, an associate professor in UTA's Department of Computer Science and Engineering who led the study, explained why this is so concerning. "Anyone can be the attacker, and that makes it scarier," Nilizadeh said. And she's right. Someone using these tools may need very little personal knowledge about you. Your public posts can provide much of the information needed to create a believable message.
Researchers show how AI turns personal details into convincing scams

The research team, which included graduate student Elham Pourabbas Vafa and researcher Sayak Saha Roy, examined how AI could analyze public social media activity and generate personalized phishing emails. According to the research paper, the team studied 200 public Instagram accounts. They found that as few as 10 posts from an individual could provide enough information to create highly targeted messages.

The researchers evaluated more than 18,000 AI-generated emails and compared them with thousands of real-world phishing messages. The AI tools pulled information from travel photos and public updates about upcoming events. They also examined personal concerns people had shared online. From there, the technology created emails that appeared relevant to each person's recent experiences. The researchers even tested how AI could customize subject lines, sender names and links to make the messages more believable.

Consider something as simple as posting that you're excited about an upcoming concert. A scammer could use that information to send a fake ticket confirmation or an offer for upgraded seats. If you had recently complained about a delayed flight, an email offering compensation might arrive at just the right moment. These examples show how easily familiar details could be turned against someone. In a user study, participants generally rated the AI-generated emails as more convincing and less suspicious than the real-world phishing examples used for comparison.

However, the researchers evaluated people's reactions to the messages in a controlled setting. They did not measure how many people would actually click the malicious links during a real attack. Even with that limitation, the results raise serious concerns about how easily personal information can be used to manipulate someone's trust.
Why personalized phishing emails are getting harder to spot

One of the most unsettling parts of this research is that scammers may never need to hack your social media account. If your profile is public, they can potentially collect details you've already shared with the world. And those details can make an otherwise suspicious message feel familiar.

An email mentioning a restaurant you visited yesterday might seem harmless. So could a message referencing a concert you attended over the weekend. When the timing and details are accurate, people may be less likely to question where the message came from. That's the advantage scammers are hoping to exploit.

This research adds another concern because AI can automate much of the work involved in creating personalized messages. There's also the problem of how polished these emails can sound. We're used to looking for spelling mistakes and awkward wording. AI can produce professional-sounding messages, so those traditional warning signs may be missing. You could receive an email that looks perfectly normal, references something you actually did and still comes from someone trying to steal your information.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Scammers can use AI to analyze your online activity and send personalized messages designed to trick you into clicking malicious links. (NickyLloyd via Getty Images)
AI safety filters missed most phishing requests

Now, you might assume AI companies already have safeguards that prevent people from using their tools to create phishing scams. They do. But the researchers found that those protections had significant weaknesses. The team tested three widely used AI safety tools: Llama Guard, ShieldGemma and WildGuard. These systems attempt to recognize harmful requests before an AI model responds.

With their default settings, the tools detected only 0% to 19% of the requests to create personalized phishing attacks. That's a pretty troubling result, especially considering how quickly AI can generate these messages.

The researchers then explored whether more specific instructions could help the safety systems recognize these attacks. The improvement was substantial. After researchers adjusted the safeguards to identify context-aware phishing attempts, detection rates reached as high as 99% in their tests. That's encouraging because it suggests stronger safeguards are possible. However, those results came from a research setting. They don't guarantee that every malicious request would be blocked in the real world.

The researchers also left the exact instructions used to generate their phishing emails out of the public paper. They wanted to avoid providing criminals with a ready-made guide. Nilizadeh is urging AI companies to take these threats seriously and improve their protections against targeted social engineering attacks.
How to protect yourself from AI phishing scams

These findings show how easily scammers could turn everyday social media posts into convincing emails. You don't need to stop sharing your life online, but it's worth being more thoughtful about what strangers can see. And there are several practical ways to protect yourself if a suspicious message reaches your inbox.

Start by checking who can see your posts on Instagram, Facebook and other social media platforms. If your accounts are public, strangers may be able to view your photos and personal updates. Consider limiting access to approved followers and reviewing older posts that reveal more than you'd like. You can follow our guide on how to change your Instagram privacy settings. Keep in mind that people can still share or screenshot content from private accounts.

Posting vacation photos while you're still away can reveal where you are. The same goes for announcing upcoming travel plans or tagging yourself at an event. Consider waiting until you're home to share certain experiences. Also, check location tags and other details in your photos before posting them publicly. You don't need to stop sharing the things you enjoy, but a little discretion can make it harder for strangers to follow your activities.

If an email arrives from a hotel or another business referencing something you recently did, don't assume it's legitimate. Open the company's official app or type its website address into your browser instead of clicking the email link. You can also contact the business through a phone number you've independently verified. Be especially suspicious when a message asks you to sign in, provide payment information or respond urgently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices if you encounter a phishing attack. Some security tools can warn you about known dangerous websites and detect malware hidden in suspicious attachments or downloads. That's valuable protection if you accidentally click something malicious. However, antivirus software cannot guarantee that every phishing website will be blocked, especially if you voluntarily enter your information. Keep your security software updated and turn on its available protection features. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
Even a simple photo shared online could give scammers clues to make a phishing email seem legitimate. (iStock)

Scammers can learn more about you than you might realize. Data brokers and people-search websites may expose your home address, phone number and other personal details that criminals could use to make phishing emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help find that information and request its removal from covered websites. While no service can erase everything about you online or remove your public social media posts, it can help reduce the personal information available to scammers. You can also request removals yourself for free, although doing so across multiple websites can take time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

A scammer who steals one password may try using it to access other accounts. That's why every important account should have a unique, strong password. A trusted password manager can help you create and store them. Enable multifactor authentication wherever possible, preferably with an authenticator app or security key. Passkeys can offer even stronger phishing resistance on supported services. And never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

Security updates help close vulnerabilities that criminals can exploit. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer and browser whenever possible. It's also worth checking that your email provider's spam and phishing filters are active. Gmail, Outlook and other major email services already block many suspicious messages, although some attacks can still get through. If you receive a suspicious email, use the built-in option to report it as phishing.
Know what to do if you click a suspicious link
Accidentally clicking a phishing link doesn't automatically mean your device has been compromised. However, if you think you've encountered a scam, here's what to do next.

Stop interacting immediately: Close the suspicious page. Don't enter personal information or download anything from the website.Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.

Scan your device: If you downloaded a file or suspect malware, run a security scan using strong antivirus software.
Change compromised passwords: If you entered a password, change it immediately through the legitimate website using a trusted device.
Review account activity: Check for unfamiliar logins or suspicious transactions. Sign out of unrecognized sessions and enable multifactor authentication.
Contact your bank: If you shared financial information, notify your bank or credit card company immediately. Ask them to help secure your accounts.
Report the scam: Report suspicious emails through your email provider and file a report with the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/.
One final suggestion. When an email seems unusually well-timed or knows something personal about you, give it a second look. That little bit of hesitation could prevent a very expensive mistake.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think most of us understand that sharing personal information online comes with some risk. But this research takes that concern in a direction many people probably haven't considered. You could share a perfectly innocent photo from dinner or a weekend getaway and later receive an email that seems to know exactly where you've been. I can see how someone might trust that message, especially if it arrives at the right time and looks like it came from a familiar business. That's what worries me. AI is making it easier for criminals to use our own experiences to earn our trust. And they may be able to do it without spending much time researching us individually. I'm encouraged that the researchers found ways to improve AI safety filters. I'd like to see companies put those findings to work. In the meantime, I think we all need to be a little more careful about what we post publicly and a lot more skeptical of unexpected emails, even when the details seem right.

title: New AI malware ranks victims by how much they're worth
summary: VOLTA-AUTODOXER malware uses AI to analyze stolen data and rank victims by potential value, helping criminals target the most profitable accounts.
story: Kurt Knutsson, the 'CyberGuy', weighs in on warnings of rising AI cyber threats after Bill Gates sounds the alarm. Gates warns of negative surprises within a year and cautions that the world is not prepared for AI upheavals.

You probably know that hackers want your passwords, credit card information and other personal details. But what if they could also figure out how much you're worth to them? That's exactly what researchers say a newly discovered malware strain is designed to do. It steals information from your computer, studies your digital life and then uses artificial intelligence to build a detailed profile of you. The goal? Help criminals decide which victims deserve more attention and which stolen accounts could bring in the most money.

The malware is called VOLTA-AUTODOXER, and researchers at Cisco Talos uncovered it through a cybersecurity research project focused on AI-powered threats. What caught my attention is how it can take everyday details about your life and turn them into something criminals could use against you. Even a food delivery receipt could help reveal where you live. Here's how this malware works, what it could reveal about you and the steps you can take to protect yourself.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY
VOLTA-AUTODOXER steals sensitive information from Windows computers, then uses artificial intelligence to assess which victims could be most valuable to criminals. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How this new AI malware works

Most information-stealing malware follows a familiar pattern. It gets onto your computer, collects whatever sensitive information it can find and sends that data back to criminals. VOLTA-AUTODOXER takes that process further by using AI to evaluate the information after collecting it. According to Cisco Talos, the Windows malware can steal saved browser passwords, payment card information and login sessions. It also targets cryptocurrency wallets and certain work-related credentials. Once it collects that information, it builds a detailed report about the person using the computer.

That report can include your location, employer and clues about your age. The malware can also collect saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. Researchers even found that it attempts to crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults. Then comes the AI component. The malware sends the information to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter. The model receives instructions to act like an intelligence analyst and determine which stolen information could be the most valuable.

Think about that for a moment. Instead of a criminal manually reviewing hundreds of stolen accounts, AI can help sort through the information and identify potentially profitable targets. And the AI analysis is optional. Even if that part fails or cannot run, the malware can still collect information and send it to the attacker.
Your food delivery history could reveal more than you think

Here's where this gets especially personal. VOLTA-AUTODOXER can search for clues about your home address, employer and financial information. Researchers found that it can also use stolen account access to examine Gmail receipts and food delivery orders. For example, the malware looks for purchase information from services such as Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also examine receipts from Amazon and other retailers. Those records may help confirm where you live.

And it goes further. Using stolen login sessions, the malware can retrieve order histories directly from Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also search Gmail for receipts from Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal. That gives criminals another way to connect your online activity to your actual identity.

The information goes well beyond your address. The malware can collect clues about your age, workplace and online accounts. It can even look at Roblox accounts to estimate the value of virtual items. Individually, some of these details might seem harmless. But when AI combines them, criminals could develop a much clearer understanding of your personal and financial life.
AI decides which stolen information could be worth money

The most concerning part of VOLTA-AUTODOXER comes after the information has been collected. The malware asks AI to create a report that ranks the victim's assets according to their potential value. Researchers found that the instructions include a section called "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH." The AI is asked to identify valuable information and assign low, medium or high rankings.

Another section called "THEIR OPSEC" examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. In other words, the malware is designed to help criminals understand what they might gain and how well someone has protected their accounts. Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model. If the model refuses the request, the malware can try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

That fallback system is especially revealing. Whoever developed the malware anticipated that an AI model might refuse to help and built a way to try another model. The malware can also send the resulting assessment to criminals through Telegram. That means an attacker could potentially receive an organized report without having to study all the stolen information personally. There's an important point here. Researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code. They have not established that criminals have successfully used these AI-generated rankings to select real-world victims for additional attacks.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
New AI-powered malware can steal saved passwords and other sensitive information from a computer, then assess how valuable that data could be to hackers. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
The malware can delete itself after stealing your data

Another concerning capability is VOLTA-AUTODOXER's ability to remove its main executable after completing its work. That could make an infection harder to investigate. However, Cisco Talos found that the malware may leave behind a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt. That file can contain a record of what the malware collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded. For security investigators, it could provide valuable clues about what happened.

There's another detail worth knowing. The malware uses the infected computer's own internet connection to contact the AI service. Researchers also found that its observed network destinations belong to third-party services rather than infrastructure owned by the attacker. That could make suspicious activity less obvious, although it does not guarantee the malware will escape detection.

Researchers also found evidence suggesting the malware was designed as a customizable product. Its developer appears to have created a system where different criminals could supply their own settings and receive a customized version. Cisco Talos believes this could make AI-powered victim profiling available to criminals who lack advanced technical skills. However, researchers have not confirmed that the malware is being sold.
What researchers still don't know

There are some important unanswered questions. Cisco Talos first observed the analyzed sample on October 11, 2026, but researchers have not established how many computers VOLTA-AUTODOXER has infected or how widely it has spread. They also have not confirmed a specific campaign distributing this malware.

That means there's no evidence in the published findings that this malware is currently infecting large numbers of everyday computer users. Still, its capabilities show how criminals could use AI to get more value from information they already know how to steal. And for now, there's no confirmed method of distribution for VOLTA-AUTODOXER. That's why it's important to focus on protecting your computer against information-stealing malware in general rather than assuming this particular threat arrives through a specific type of message or download.
How to protect yourself from AI-powered malware

You don't need to understand how AI works to reduce your risk. VOLTA-AUTODOXER still needs access to your computer before it can collect sensitive information. That means many of the same precautions that protect against traditional malware can help here, too. Here are some practical steps worth taking.

One of the best ways to protect yourself is to have strong antivirus software running on your devices. Good security software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious programs and other threats before they steal your information. Keep your protection updated and run regular scans. Look for software that monitors suspicious behavior in addition to scanning for known threats. That's especially helpful when dealing with malware designed to hide its activity or delete itself after an attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER specifically targets credentials stored in web browsers. Consider using a reputable password manager that protects your passwords in an encrypted vault instead. Create a strong, unique password for every important account. That way, one stolen password won't automatically give criminals access to other services. However, a password manager alone cannot guarantee protection if your computer has already been compromised. Some malware can steal active login sessions or capture sensitive information while you're using it.

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services. Whenever possible, use passkeys or a hardware security key. However, remember that some information-stealing malware can steal active login sessions. That means 2FA alone may not stop every account takeover. If you suspect an infection, sign out of existing sessions after securing your device.

Install Windows security updates and keep your browser current. Updates can close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to install malware. Also, avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites. Be especially cautious about unexpected attachments or messages urging you to install something immediately. And never copy commands into Windows PowerShell, Command Prompt or the Run dialog because a random website tells you to fix a problem. Criminals have used these tactics to trick people into installing other information-stealing malware.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Cisco Talos researchers uncovered malware that can steal passwords, payment information and login sessions before using AI to build a profile of its victim. (Pornyot Palilai via Getty Images)

VOLTA-AUTODOXER shows how seemingly unrelated personal details can help criminals build a profile of you. Consider using a personal data removal service to reduce the information that data brokers publish about you. These services cannot erase information already stolen from your computer. However, they can help reduce the amount of personal information available through public data broker listings. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Because this malware collects financial and identifying information, consider using an identity theft protection service. Such services can monitor for certain signs of misuse and alert you to suspicious activity. You should also review your financial statements and credit reports regularly. If criminals gain access to your information, early detection could help limit the damage. You can also place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. That can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name, even if they've stolen personal information. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER can also target information connected to your workplace. That includes certain Microsoft account tokens, cloud credentials and Slack workspace details. If you use your computer for work, avoid storing sensitive access keys in unprotected files. Follow your company's security policies and report suspicious activity to your IT department immediately. Cisco Talos also identified a technique that attempts to bypass Chrome's App-Bound Encryption protection. Organizations can reduce that risk by controlling which programs can launch Chrome in headless mode. That is a more technical safeguard your IT or security team can evaluate.
What to do if you think your computer has been infected
If you suspect malware has stolen your information, act quickly.

Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.
Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.

Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.

Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.

Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.

Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.

Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.

Most importantly, don't assume you're safe because the suspicious program has disappeared. This malware can delete itself after stealing your information, and the stolen credentials may still be usable by criminals.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about VOLTA-AUTODOXER is how much someone could learn about you just by getting into your computer. Think about what's sitting on your device right now. Maybe you've saved a few passwords in your browser. Your email probably contains years of receipts, including orders delivered right to your front door. Now, consider what happens when a criminal feeds all that information into AI and asks one simple question: How much is this person worth? That's what caught my attention about this research. The malware is designed to do the homework for the criminal and help identify which stolen information deserves the most attention. We still don't know how widely VOLTA-AUTODOXER has spread, so there's no reason to assume your computer has been targeted. But I do think this gives us a pretty good idea of where cybercrime could be heading. The less work criminals have to do themselves, the easier it could become for them to target more people. And that's one more reason to take your personal information seriously before someone gets hold of it.

How would you feel knowing that hackers could use AI to put a dollar value on your personal information? And do you think AI companies should do more to prevent criminals from using their technology this way? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: New big rig safety tech could save your life
summary: Daimler Truck's Oregon demos show how a Freightliner Cascadia's automatic emergency braking responds when dummy cars suddenly cross a moving truck's path.
story: Daimler Truck's advanced safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor surrounding vehicles and help prevent dangerous collisions. (Joe Raedle/Newsmakers via Getty Images)

Ever find yourself driving next to a massive 18-wheeler and wondering if the driver can actually see your car? It's a reasonable concern. Big rigs have enormous blind spots, and stopping one takes a lot more time and distance than stopping your car. Now, new big rig safety tech from Daimler Truck could help prevent some of the most dangerous crashes on our roads.

The company behind Freightliner is upgrading its trucks with technology that can recognize potential collisions and automatically hit the brakes. We're talking about situations where another driver suddenly cuts across a truck's path or a pedestrian gets dangerously close during a turn. And demonstrations at Daimler's Oregon proving grounds offer a revealing look at what happens when this technology faces situations that could turn deadly on public roads.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
What happens when a car suddenly cuts in front of a big rig?

At Daimler Truck's testing facility in Oregon, engineers recreated situations that could easily turn deadly on a public road. They used dummy cars mounted on remote-controlled platforms to simulate vehicles suddenly crossing in front of a moving Freightliner Cascadia. In one demonstration, the truck successfully avoided a collision. In another, it clipped the dummy car after braking. That second test may sound like a failure, but consider what could have happened if the truck had continued at full speed. Slowing down before impact can make an enormous difference when a passenger car comes face-to-face with a fully loaded truck.

The demonstrations generally took place at speeds between 40 and 55 mph. Daimler said the truck's trailer carried approximately 30,000 pounds during the tests. That's a lot of weight pushing forward when the brakes suddenly engage. And here's what caught my attention. The technology was designed to recognize these developing dangers and respond even when the driver had little time to react. That's especially important because a few seconds can determine how serious a collision becomes.
How big rig safety tech spots trouble before a crash

The technology comes from Detroit Assurance, Daimler Truck North America's collection of advanced driver assistance systems. At the center is Active Brake Assist 6, also known as ABA6. It uses five radar sensors and a camera to monitor what's happening around the truck. Together, they provide approximately 270 degrees of coverage, including areas alongside a standard 53-foot trailer.

Think of it as another set of electronic eyes helping the driver keep track of nearby traffic. The system can identify certain vehicles that have stopped unexpectedly, including cars sitting at unusual angles after an accident. For example, a truck approaching a crash scene might encounter a disabled vehicle partly blocking the roadway. Active Brake Assist 6 is designed to recognize these situations and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes.

The technology can recognize pedestrians and cyclists in certain scenarios, too. That's particularly useful when a large truck travels through busy areas where people may be difficult to see from the cab. And Daimler is now expanding those capabilities to address another dangerous situation.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS?
Freightliner’s latest safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor traffic around big rigs and respond when a collision threat develops. (Stock Photos)
New Freightliner safety systems can brake at intersections

Intersections can be especially challenging for truck drivers. They have to maneuver a massive vehicle while watching traffic that may approach from several directions. All it takes is one person making an unexpected move. That's where a new feature called Cross Traffic Assist comes in. The system uses radar to detect vehicles crossing the truck's path at intersections. If it recognizes a potential collision, it can alert the driver with audible and visual warnings. When the danger becomes more serious, it can also apply partial or full braking. Now, think about what that could mean if someone accidentally pulls out in front of an approaching truck. The system may give the driver extra time to respond or help reduce the force of a collision.

Another improvement involves Active Side Guard Assist 2. The enhanced system adds protection when the truck makes a left turn across oncoming traffic. With the left turn signal activated, it can recognize certain approaching vehicles and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The new left-turn protection builds on existing safety technology that monitors the passenger-side blind spot during right turns. That system can detect pedestrians and cyclists and apply braking when necessary.

These improvements are scheduled to become standard on Freightliner Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with production planned for January. Active Brake Assist 6 itself is already standard on the fifth-generation Cascadia. According to Daimler Truck North America, the goal is to give professional drivers additional support when visibility or reaction time becomes limited.
What if a truck driver suddenly stops responding?

There's another feature that deserves attention because it addresses a frightening possibility. What happens if someone behind the wheel of a big rig suddenly becomes unresponsive? Freightliner's optional Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended drifting. It can also provide steering assistance during certain challenging driving conditions, such as strong crosswinds.

But the feature I find particularly interesting is called Attentive Driver Protection. When the lane-keeping system is active, Attentive Driver Protection monitors whether the driver continues responding. If the driver fails to respond to escalating warnings, the technology can slow the truck to a stop while helping keep it centered in its lane. It can also activate the hazard lights to warn surrounding traffic.

Consider the potential consequences of a driver becoming unresponsive while operating a massive truck on a busy highway. Having an additional safety system that can help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop could make a significant difference. However, the feature doesn't diagnose medical emergencies or determine why a driver has stopped responding. It reacts to a lack of driver response under specific conditions. And like the other safety systems, it still depends on factors such as road conditions and sensor performance.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
Freightliner’s Attentive Driver Protection can slow a truck to a stop if the driver stops responding to escalating warnings. (Noah Berger, File/AP Photo)
What this means to you

You may never drive a Freightliner, but chances are you share the road with big rigs regularly. And that's why these improvements should interest you. If a truck can recognize a dangerous situation and begin braking before the driver has time to react, the people in nearby vehicles could have a better chance of avoiding serious injuries. Even reducing the speed of an unavoidable collision could make a significant difference.

But don't assume every truck you encounter has these features. Many older trucks won't have the newest technology, and even equipped vehicles have limitations. Sensors can struggle in poor weather or when visibility becomes limited. Automatic braking also cannot guarantee that every collision will be avoided.

So, continue giving big rigs plenty of room. Avoid lingering beside a truck where the driver might have trouble seeing you. And when passing, make sure there's sufficient space before moving back into its lane. Remember that even the smartest technology cannot change the physics of a massive truck traveling at highway speed. The safest approach is to stay alert and avoid putting yourself in a situation where a truck driver has to make a sudden move.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what I find encouraging about Daimler's latest safety technology. It recognizes something we all know about driving. People make mistakes. Someone misjudges an intersection or pulls out without realizing how quickly a truck is approaching. Those split-second decisions can have terrible consequences, especially when a massive vehicle has little room to stop. The demonstrations in Oregon showed why this technology has potential. In one scenario, the truck avoided a collision. In another, contact still occurred, but the braking reduced the impact. That second result is an important reminder that a safety system can still provide protection even when it cannot prevent every accident. I also think we're seeing an interesting shift in how truck manufacturers approach safety. There's been plenty of attention on trucks that can drive themselves. Yet here we have technology designed to help professional drivers do their jobs more safely. And when you consider how many trucks share our highways, even modest improvements in collision prevention could have an enormous impact. Of course, controlled demonstrations are one thing. Everyday traffic brings unexpected challenges that are much harder to predict. I'll be interested to see how these systems perform as more equipped trucks reach the road. If the technology can prevent serious crashes, that's something we can all appreciate.

Would you feel safer knowing an 18-wheeler could automatically brake to avoid hitting your car, or would you still be nervous driving alongside a massive truck that relies on software to react? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
