title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
summary: How an NBC News data investigation tracked vaccination and school exemption rates across thousands of counties in the U.S.
story: Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.
For Subscribers

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.
Methodology

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.
The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.
For Subscribers
After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:
Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful.
Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions.

MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates.
Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.
With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.All data was checked for accuracy.
Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.
Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.
All data was checked for accuracy.

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers. In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.

Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers.

In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.

Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.
Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.

Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.
Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

title: Bernie Sanders says he won’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
summary: Sens. Sanders and Elissa Slotkin called for new leadership, but neither proposed an alternative. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is considering challenging Schumer.
story: WASHINGTON — Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced Tuesday he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be majority leader for the next two years after Democrats’ big 2026 victories.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said at a news conference.

Sanders, who is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, becomes a high-profile opponent with inside power and grassroots clout when it comes to Schumer’s staying on as leader.

Schumer has spent a decade as caucus leader and is vying for another two years after having led his party to a net pickup of at least seven Senate seats in the midterm elections, with Mississippi and Alaska still counting votes as two more prospects. Senate Democrats won’t elect their new leadership until next month.

The progressive wing of the party has been calling for Schumer to step aside, while some new Democratic senators haven’t committed to support him. He’ll need a majority of the caucus to win another term as leader.
Standing next to Sanders at Tuesday’s news conference was Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who has similarly called for a change of leadership without backing an alternative candidate.

“I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change,” she said. “I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership. ... It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., whom grassroots progressive advocates are drafting to challenge Schumer, said Tuesday he’s still “actively listening” to colleagues about a potential run.
But he wouldn’t say whether he’ll jump in the race.

“We should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen told reporters in the Capitol. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan, and as you know, there are many people who think change is required.”

Until a challenger jumps in and gains traction, Schumer is the clear favorite to win and become majority leader. Despite grumbling in his own caucus, Senate Republican leader John Thune of South Dakota was re-elected by his colleagues Tuesday after detractors failed to recruit an opponent.

“Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday afternoon. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it as majority leader.”
Some Democrats credit his role in the election victories and believe he deserves the post.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters. “Chuck and I have had our differences, but at the end of the day, it’s time to unify.”
Asked whether he’s supporting Schumer for majority leader, former and returning Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio replied simply: “Yes.”

Sanders wouldn’t say when he was asked by NBC News whether he favors abolishing the filibuster for the upcoming two-year session, a cause that some on the left are pushing for. It would allow Democrats to pass most legislation without any Republican support, but the same power could be used against them the next time the GOP takes the majority.

“That’s a very important question, and I haven’t reached an answer on it. I think there are a lot of reasons to support it, and that is the majority — we believe the majority rule, not necessarily having 40 people be able to deny what the majority wants,” Sanders said. “I am worried about protecting minority rights, as well.”

Sanders pointed to the “reconciliation” process, which allows the majority party to pass some legislation on its own, as long as it’s related to spending and taxes; Republicans used the process to pass President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”
“What I do believe, absolutely,” Sanders continued, “is that we can, with a major budget reconciliation bill, do a whole lot.”

title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
summary: NBC News projects that Salazar defeated her Democratic opponent in a heavily Hispanic, Miami-based district that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.
story: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after having clashed with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, tried to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”
But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns about impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview in which García told The Miami Herald, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the country. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.
Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.
In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including planned attack against U.K. airbase
summary: One of the men helped direct the planned attack against the air base while he was in a U.S. prison, according to a Justice Department indictment.
story: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.
Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.
“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.
Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.
In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.
His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.

The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.
The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

title: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
summary: The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the ⁠city of Gloucester, ​in the west ⁠of England, British police said.
story: LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the ⁠city of Gloucester, ​in the west ⁠of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in London.

He was ​arrested ⁠on suspicion of ‌offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, ‌the statement said. They relate to obtaining ‌or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement added.
Three people familiar with the matter told NBC News that the soldier was based at NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters at Imjin Barracks on the outskirts of Gloucester.
A senior NATO military official also confirmed the location of the soldier’s assignment.
“We can confirm that the American service member arrested by British police was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC),” the official said in a statement.
For Subscribers

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and that it “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, was quoted in the police statement as saying, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”said.
For Subscribers

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”
Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Britain’s senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counterterrorism operations, the statement said.
The arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson fires and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
The U.S. has moved military aircraft from an air base in the U.K. amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Osprey tilt-rotor military transports left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

title:
Call her candid: Sofia Franklyn’s memoir details 
Alex Cooper fallout
summary: “Daddy Issues” is a tell-all from Franklyn’s side about the end of her business relationship and friendship with Cooper, who went on to helm “Call Her Daddy” solo.
story: The “Daddy Gang” is finally getting to hear from the co-“founding father” of “Call Her Daddy.”
Sofia Franklyn, who co-created the famous podcast with Alex Cooper, on Tuesday released her memoir, “Daddy Issues,” in which she details her falling-out with her now ex-friend.

The duo shot to viral fame in 2018, when the podcast was still under Barstool Sports. It became known for candid conversations about commonly taboo topics for women to discuss publicly, including raunchy sex stories.

But the two professionally split up in 2020, news that initially shocked their listeners. Cooper went on to host the podcast solo, eventually moving it to Spotify and now SiriusXM in lucrative deals that helped propel her to mainstream success.
Meanwhile, Franklyn, who is an influencer with over 619,000 Instagram followers, launched her own podcast titled “Sofia with an F.”
Over the years, rumors had circulated about what exactly happened between Franklyn and Cooper. Here are some of the biggest claims in Franklyn’s 240-page book.
Warnings from others in Cooper’s orbit

Franklyn writes about struggling to find a clear path as she was growing up in Utah with a single mom. She was arrested three times: once for using a fake ID and twice for underage drinking. Eventually, she left to start anew in New York City, largely to escape an abusive relationship.

But her early days in the city were far from ideal. She lived with her aunt and was working at Morgan Stanley in a job under a toxic boss who she claims harassed her regularly. She eventually moved into her own place, which she could barely afford, and found herself feeling extremely lonely.
Until she met Cooper.
A random girl Franklyn befriended in a ride-share connected her to Cooper and her childhood friend Lauren, who were looking for a third roommate.

Cooper and Franklyn ended up becoming inseparable, with Lauren largely out of the picture as she spent much of her time with her boyfriend. But one night, Franklyn writes, she and Lauren shared a rare evening in the apartment alone together.
That’s when Lauren asked Franklyn whether she thought it was weird that Cooper had “tossed” her aside.
“You showed up and it was like I never existed,” Franklyn said Lauren told her, which prompted Franklyn to apologize.
Lauren also told Franklyn that Cooper “uses you because you’re hot, to like, go to parties and stuff.”
At the time, Franklyn wrote, she felt defensive of her friendship with Cooper and did not think of Cooper as “using” her.
But later, another close friend of Cooper’s from childhood also seemed to warn her that Cooper was not going to stick with her.
Muji, known to early “Call Her Daddy” listeners as “Milfhunter,” worked on the podcast with the duo. He told Franklyn that Cooper “doesn’t have friends. I’ve watched it happen since high school.”
When Cooper abruptly fired Muji, Franklyn said, he told her: “She’s gonna f--- you.”
An alleged firing attempt, secret raise and IP disagreement
Cooper and Franklyn’s stars rose quickly at Barstool as the two took creative control of their show with company founder Dave Portnoy’s blessing.
But Franklyn started to feel things change after the Barstool holiday party. That night, she felt “insane anxiety,” drank excessively and fought with Cooper.
An angry Cooper told Franklyn she was “rude” and “aggressive” toward her at the party and that everyone, including Portnoy, had noticed and wanted to fire her.

Franklyn says she wanted to apologize to Portnoy for her behavior but was told not to by Cooper. When she finally did say something, Portnoy appeared to dismiss it, saying that “the girls got in a fight.”
It wasn’t until later, Franklyn writes, that she learned Cooper had used the party as a way to negotiate a raise for herself.
Muji purportedly told her that Cooper said, “If I have to put up with her, I need more money.” She got the raise: $20,000 more than Franklyn every year.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“She didn’t tell you because she didn’t want you to know she tried to get you fired,” Franklyn said Muji told her.

Franklyn writes that in 2020, when the duo were negotiating their new contract together, they sent Barstool an email with a new proposal asking for a “50/50 split of all revenue derived from Barstool’s exploitation of the property (i.e., advertisers, sponsors, merch, etc.)” and a “minimum guarantee — $1M each, per year.”
The negotiations centered on the intellectual property for “Call Her Daddy,” which Barstool Sports owned and could technically continue without Franklyn or Cooper attached.

Amid their talks with Barstool, Franklyn said, she and Cooper agreed their goal was to stay together. They even came up with a spinoff podcast in case the negotiations fell through, titling it “The Fathers.”

“We’re being corny as s---, but it’s because we’re both blissed out on the plan and our future — we don’t know how Barstool will respond, but we know that staying together is more important than losing the IP, or whatever they may threaten. What is the name without us?”
But in the end, Franklyn was ousted as co-host. Portnoy called Franklyn to tell her that Cooper had met with him separately and proposed going on without her.

“She came to me with a plan, and I needed an episode. There’s no clear favorite,” he told her, according to Franklyn’s memoir. “You could always have your own show, and we promote the s--- out of it like we did with Call Her Daddy. I think it would be huge.”
Portnoy also said Cooper had hired her own lawyer and claimed that Franklyn had been “the one that’s been dragging this on, and she’s been ready to sign this thing.”

Franklyn claims Cooper subsequently locked her out of their shared social accounts and posted a 52-minute YouTube breakup video called “The Truth about Call Her Daddy” in which she described Franklyn as a “liability.” Six years later, the video is still up, and it has amassed 4.6 million views.
Representatives for Portnoy and Cooper did not respond to requests for comment Tuesday.
Cooper’s alleged legal threat
The book opens with a scene in which Franklyn’s book agent calls her to say she had received an angry call from Matt Kaplan.
Kaplan, a Hollywood producer, married Cooper in 2024. The couple co-founded the Unwell Network, a subsidiary of the media company Trending.
Franklyn writes that her agent told her Kaplan said Cooper would sue.
Representatives from Unwell told The New York Times that Kaplan “never discussed the book’s claims or any intent to sue the author with Verve.”
A representative for Kaplan did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

title: Kennedy family members seek to block construction of Trump’s arch
summary: Nine family members seek to join a lawsuit against the arch, arguing it would cast a shadow over the site where some of their notable relatives are buried.
story: Nine members of the Kennedy family asked a federal judge in Washington on Tuesday for permission to join the legal battle against President Donald Trump’s planned “triumphal” arch, arguing the structure would cast a shadow over some of their relatives’ graves.

The Kennedys said the arch’s planned location in the nation’s capital would also obstruct the clear sight line from the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame memorial across the Arlington Memorial Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, which the family called “an essential element” of the design.

The high-profile request once again pits one of the most storied families in American history against Trump. The two sides have also sparred over Trump’s attempt to remake the Kennedy Center. Trump closed the arts institution after a judge blocked him from adding his name to the building.
The Kennedys asking to join the suit include seven of Robert F. Kennedy’s living children — all except Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

In a statement, Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said the request was about “protecting sacred spaces,” adding that they believed Trump had “violated the laws and procedures established by Congress to protect this most sacred national memorial.”

“A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come,” the statement said.

The District of Columbia and Virginia, as well as Vietnam War veteran and former U.S. ambassador Michael Lemmon, had sued over the project. The Kennedys asked to join both suits, arguing they have a “direct, immediate stake in this matter and claims that share common questions of law.”

The arch is set to be built on Memorial Circle, between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. It is designed to stand at 250 feet tall, more than twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial.
A federal judge blocked construction on the project last week, shortly after a planning board with a majority of Trump-aligned members voted to approve it.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Kennedy family members buried at Arlington include President John F. Kennedy, first lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy.
The Kennedys asking to join the suit argue they have “a unique interest” in the property.

“As members of the Kennedy family, intervenors have a particular interest in protecting the Kennedy Gravesites, ensuring that these Gravesites remain unimpeded as a solemn and sacred memorial to the legacy of the Kennedy family,” they wrote.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in response to the suit that the administration is “confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”

“It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery,” Ingle said in a statement. “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”

title: 3 dead, 3 critically injured after vehicle smashes into pedestrians in Los Angeles
summary: LOS ANGELES — Three people were killed when a vehicle careened into pedestrians near a public transportation stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening, officials said.
story: LOS ANGELES — Three people were killed when a vehicle careened into pedestrians near a public transportation stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening, officials said.

Los Angeles police said a white SUV struck at least five pedestrians at Lankershim and Chandler boulevards in the North Hollywood section of the city, where a Los Angeles Metro station is located, at around 5:55 p.m.
Three others were taken to the hospital in critical condition, the Los Angeles Fire Department said.

The SUV’s driver, a man in his mid-60s, was among the injured, Police Capt. Warner Castillo said. The department’s drug-recognition experts were at the hospital to determine whether the driver was impaired, he said.
Police did not believe that any other vehicle was involved, Castillo said.
The fire department said the three people who were killed were beyond medical help when first responders arrived and were declared dead at the scene.

Assistant Fire Chief Joe Everett told reporters that an agency battalion chief came across the crash at around 6 p.m., “and what he found was a car that had careened into a number of people on the sidewalk.”
Everyone who was struck was on the sidewalk, Police Chief Jim McDonnell said, noting that the investigation is still in its early stages.
Mayor Karen Bass said the people who were struck were pedestrians and vendors. She said her office is coordinating with city departments and authorities to determine the cause of the crash.
“I’m heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted. We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available,” Bass said.

Aerial video from NBC Los Angeles showed what appeared to be a white vehicle crashed into the side of the Metro station, which houses escalators and stairs that go down to the subway, and debris scattered over the area.
“It was a huge boom,” Lincoln Brown, who was walking away from the station at the time, told NBC Los Angeles.
“I was walking the opposite direction, but I heard a loud crash behind me,” he said. “I turn around, and I see a car that’s smashed up against the Metro over there.”
A witness said two women selling hot dogs were thrown in the air from the impact, the station reported.
It was not clear how fast the vehicle was traveling, and investigators will be looking at video and interviewing witnesses, McDonnell said.
“It’ll be probably a prolonged but very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here, and our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight,” he said.
Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors member Kathryn Barger expressed her condolences and wishes for the recovery of those injured.
“I am stunned by the tragic loss of life in North Hollywood and my thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this devastating incident,” she said in a statement.

title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including planned attack against U.K. airbase
summary: One of the men helped direct the planned attack against the air base while he was in a U.S. prison, according to a Justice Department indictment.
story: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.
Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.
“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.
Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.
In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.
His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.

The indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.
The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

title: How North Carolina emerged as one of Democrats’ biggest midterm bright spots: From the Politics Desk
summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki digs into battleground North Carolina’s massive midterm shift toward Democrats.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki digs into battleground North Carolina’s massive midterm shift toward Democrats. Plus, our Capitol Hill team has the latest on the Republican leadership elections.
— Adam Wollner
🚨Breaking news: The Republican-led House narrowly rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Read more →
How North Carolina emerged as one of Democrats’ biggest midterm bright spots
With so many competing storylines and surprising outcomes from last week’s midterms, it may have been easy to miss what happened in North Carolina.

Democrats have so far managed to flip five seats from red to blue in the Tar Heel State, tied for the most of any state in the country with California, where a redrawn map gave the party a boost. And with three House races still uncalled in North Carolina, there could be more.

Razor-thin margins separate two Republican incumbents, Reps. Greg Murphy and Virginia Foxx, and their Democratic challengers in the 3rd and 5th districts, respectively. And in the 7th District, GOP Rep. David Rouzer is up by roughly 2,500 votes.
This is all happening in a state that hasn’t gone for a Democrat in a presidential race since Barack Obama in 2008, and one that President Donald Trump carried by 3 points in 2024.
But last week, former Gov. Roy Cooper anchored the party’s efforts at the top of the ticket, sailing to victory over former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley by nearly 20 points.

This swing occurred even after Republicans drew a new congressional map in 2025, when they aimed to extend their advantage from 10-4 to 11-3. The mid-decade redistricting effort, spurred on by Trump, backfired spectacularly, as it did in other states.

In addition to the five flips — all in districts Trump carried by at least 9 points in 2024 — Democratic Rep. Don Davis held on to the seat in the 1st District the GOP was targeting by 3 points. And one of the seats Democrats gained is held by Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of House Republicans’ national campaign arm.

Kian Sadjadi, the executive director of the North Carolina Democratic Party, said he was still studying the results, but that the largest discernible shift he saw came from young, male voters who broke toward Democrats after backing Trump in 2024. Unaffiliated and inconsistent voters overwhelmingly went with Democrats as well, he said.
“We had a big increase in our turnout overall. We saw turnout coming from all parts of the state — basically, every single county except for a couple moved toward the Democrats,” Sadjadi said.

For years, North Carolina Democrats have credited state party Chair Anderson Clayton for building up a strong on-the-ground organization. In recent cycles, that has meant flipping statewide, judicial and local seats.
Now, North Carolina Democrats will hold a majority of the state’s congressional seats and have a newly minted senator.
What does it mean for the 2028 presidential election?

“I don’t think that we can look at this year as kind of a bellwether for ’28. We’re still going to have to work hard every day … we’re still going to have to fight like we’re behind and not take this as a surefire path to victory,” Sadjadi said.
But, he added, “We will be a true battleground. It’ll be one of our most competitive states.”
🗳️ Related read: The House districts that remain uncalled after the 2026 midterms, by Sarah Sternhagen
House Republicans elect Rep. Jim Jordan as their next leader following election losses
After a blue tidal wave swept them from power, House Republicans elected a new GOP leader to replace outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson.
For Subscribers

House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., a close Johnson ally, for minority leader, two Republican lawmakers said. The vote was held behind closed doors and by secret ballot.
For Subscribers
The vote was 106-73, the two lawmakers in the room said.

Jordan is a fervent supporter of President Donald Trump and had pitched to GOP colleagues that his past role chairing the Oversight Committee would allow him to combat the spate of investigations newly empowered Democrats have promised to launch into Trump’s administration, family and business ventures.
“I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” he wrote to his colleagues.
Jordan’s victory signals that House Republicans wanted a clean break from the Johnson political apparatus following last week’s historic GOP drubbing.

It’s a remarkable ascent for Jordan, who has spent two decades in Congress and had once been considered a conservative bomb-thrower who often clashed with the GOP leadership team, though the ambitious Republican has become more of a team player in recent years as he led House committees.

On the other side of the Capitol: Senate Republicans also held their leadership elections today, re-electing their current leadership slate after a small group of conservatives had pushed to delay the election. Sen. John Thune of South Dakota will serve as minority leader in the next Congress.

As for the Democrats: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be majority leader. He appeared at a news conference today alongside Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who has similarly called for a change of leadership without backing an alternative candidate.

“I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change,” she said. “I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership. ... It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election.”

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., whom grassroots progressive advocates are drafting to challenge Schumer, said he’s still “actively listening” to colleagues about a potential run. But he wouldn’t say whether he’ll jump in the race.

“We should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen told reporters in the Capitol. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan, and as you know, there are many people who think change is required.”

Until a challenger jumps in and gains traction, Schumer is the clear favorite to maintain his perch at the top of the Senate Democratic caucus. The party’s leadership elections are slated to take place next month.

title: Missing baby found alive buried in dog crate in South Carolina
summary: The Lexington County sheriff said the crate most likely provided enough air for 11-month-old Koah Sharpe to survive.
story: An 11-month-old boy who officials said was taken by his father on Monday was found buried alive in a dog crate Tuesday, a discovery a South Carolina sheriff called “joyful.”
Koah Sharpe was found alive in a dog crate that was wrapped in a towel, Lexington County Sheriff Bryan Koon told reporters.
“That, by the grace of God, probably provided enough air for him to survive — our estimation is for the last 24 hours under that dirt,” he said.
Koah, described as a 20-pound boy with reddish hair who had a pacifier, was taken by his father, Michael Comer, on Monday morning, the sheriff’s office said.
The crate was found around 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, Koon said, near the home of Comer’s father.
Comer was arrested late Monday in Lexington County on a burglary charge after he was found in an outbuilding. The baby was not with him, the sheriff’s office said.
Koon said Comer’s mother was taking care of the baby Monday morning. Comer came over and his mother left, but another caregiver was on the way, Koon said.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” he said.
Comer’s mother, Patricia Comer, said in a phone interview Tuesday that she was shocked and that her son’s being in police custody was “where he needs to be.”
“Honestly, I’m his mother, and I never expected this from him,” she said.

Koah’s mother has full custody of the child, Patricia Comer said. But the boy’s mother would let Patricia Comer supervise him on weekends, and there was no custody agreement preventing Michael Comer from watching the child unsupervised, which he had done before with no problems, Patricia Comer said.

She said she went to work Monday and left Koah in his father’s care. Then, at around 11 a.m., a friend went to the home to drop off some formula but no one answered, prompting the friend to call her, Patricia Comer recalled.
“Something just did not feel right. I told my boss, ‘I need to leave work,’” she said. “Call it mother’s instinct. I don’t know what it was.”
For Subscribers
She went home and, “sure enough, Michael had left,” she said.
The child was reported missing, and law enforcement began a search.
Deputies went to Comer’s father’s home Monday and found the doors open and baby belongings in the house but no sign of Comer or the child, Koon said.
The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, the FBI and the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were part of the search for the child.
For Subscribers
A search party of nearly 100 police officers, firefighters and other officials looked for the boy, Koon said.
Searchers found a site Tuesday not far from Comer’s father’s house, about 50 yards into some woods with freshly disturbed earth, Koon said.
“As they probed it and laid it out and started digging, you could hear little Koah crying,” he said. “So, as you can imagine, the race was on.”
The baby was taken to a hospital, where he was being cared for Tuesday afternoon, Koon said. He said he hopes the child makes a full recovery.
“He was screaming at the top of his lungs, which is a good thing in the baby world, I would guess,” Koon said.
The wire crate, which was about 2 feet by 2 feet, was buried in a shallow hole, Koon said. Wrapping it in a towel probably created an air pocket, he said.
Koon said authorities were working with the prosecutor’s office regarding charges. It was not immediately clear whether Comer had an attorney who could speak on his behalf.
Koon said the cool weather may also have helped the baby’s chances of survival.
“A lot of things were going in Koah’s favor, and the good Lord looked down on him the last 24 hours,” he said.
Patricia Comer said that what her son is accused of doing is “pure evil” and that there were no warning signs.
She said her son lives with her after a recent jail stint for having drunkenly gone to the home of an ex of Koah’s mother. She added that “all he does is go to work and come home.”
She also said she feels hurt that some people are blaming her.
“Just know that if I could have prevented this, I would have done everything in my power,” Patricia Comer said. “I had no idea this was going to happen.”
She thanked the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department and all the agencies and officials who helped find her grandson alive.
“I did not know he would do anything like this,” she said of her son. “He’s always been so good with Koah. Who would think their own child would do something like this?”

title: Bernie Sanders says he won’t support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader
summary: Sens. Sanders and Elissa Slotkin called for new leadership, but neither proposed an alternative. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is considering challenging Schumer.
story: WASHINGTON — Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., announced Tuesday he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be majority leader for the next two years after Democrats’ big 2026 victories.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said at a news conference.

Sanders, who is in line to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, becomes a high-profile opponent with inside power and grassroots clout when it comes to Schumer’s staying on as leader.

Schumer has spent a decade as caucus leader and is vying for another two years after having led his party to a net pickup of at least seven Senate seats in the midterm elections, with Mississippi and Alaska still counting votes as two more prospects. Senate Democrats won’t elect their new leadership until next month.

The progressive wing of the party has been calling for Schumer to step aside, while some new Democratic senators haven’t committed to support him. He’ll need a majority of the caucus to win another term as leader.
Standing next to Sanders at Tuesday’s news conference was Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who has similarly called for a change of leadership without backing an alternative candidate.

“I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change,” she said. “I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership. ... It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., whom grassroots progressive advocates are drafting to challenge Schumer, said Tuesday he’s still “actively listening” to colleagues about a potential run.
But he wouldn’t say whether he’ll jump in the race.

“We should not have a coronation,” Van Hollen told reporters in the Capitol. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan, and as you know, there are many people who think change is required.”

Until a challenger jumps in and gains traction, Schumer is the clear favorite to win and become majority leader. Despite grumbling in his own caucus, Senate Republican leader John Thune of South Dakota was re-elected by his colleagues Tuesday after detractors failed to recruit an opponent.

“Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday afternoon. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it as majority leader.”
Some Democrats credit his role in the election victories and believe he deserves the post.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give them another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters. “Chuck and I have had our differences, but at the end of the day, it’s time to unify.”
Asked whether he’s supporting Schumer for majority leader, former and returning Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio replied simply: “Yes.”

Sanders wouldn’t say when he was asked by NBC News whether he favors abolishing the filibuster for the upcoming two-year session, a cause that some on the left are pushing for. It would allow Democrats to pass most legislation without any Republican support, but the same power could be used against them the next time the GOP takes the majority.

“That’s a very important question, and I haven’t reached an answer on it. I think there are a lot of reasons to support it, and that is the majority — we believe the majority rule, not necessarily having 40 people be able to deny what the majority wants,” Sanders said. “I am worried about protecting minority rights, as well.”

Sanders pointed to the “reconciliation” process, which allows the majority party to pass some legislation on its own, as long as it’s related to spending and taxes; Republicans used the process to pass President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.”
“What I do believe, absolutely,” Sanders continued, “is that we can, with a major budget reconciliation bill, do a whole lot.”

title: Republican-led House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
summary: The Republican-led House rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over how he has carried out the war in Iran and other military hostilities.
story: WASHINGTON — The Republican-led House on Tuesday narrowly rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over how he has carried out the war in Iran and other military hostilities in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

The vote was 211-204 to send the impeachment resolution to committee, effectively killing the effort. Even vocal GOP critics of Hegseth said they didn’t think that the secretary’s action rose to the level of “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

The impeachment resolution was authored by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a fierce critic of Hegseth and President Donald Trump; both helped oust Massie in his GOP primary race earlier this year. Because Massie had filed the motion as “privileged,” Republican leaders were forced to call a vote within two legislative days.

Hegseth “has violated the norms of war, and it’s to the disadvantage and the dishonor of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflicts,” said Massie, the lone Republican who voted with Democrats to keep the impeachment resolution alive on Tuesday.

“Somebody’s got to put their foot down and say, ‘Are we going to follow the laws that are on the books? Are we going to follow the Constitution?’” he continued. “And the best way to do that is to have an impeachment against Pete Hegseth.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is on track to be elected speaker in January, has said Democrats will “run Pete Hegseth out of town” when they take over Congress next year.
But Hegseth is safe for now, and Trump said he is standing by his defense secretary, who has clashed with not only Democrats but a handful of Republicans in the Senate and the House.
The vote came at the end of a dramatic day in Washington that Hegseth kicked off with a morning news conference at the Pentagon, where he slammed the impeachment as a “political spectacle.”
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.

He argued that all of the military actions cited by Massie were “lawful” and called the impeachment a direct affront to the men and women carrying out those missions. Hegseth also equated Tuesday’s impeachment vote to the two Democratic-led votes to impeach Trump during his first term — first over a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the second over the Jan. 6 attack at the Capitol.
“If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week,” Hegseth said.

Shortly after Hegseth’s appearance, Trump posted his support for the defense secretary on Truth Social, saying he “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Trump posted again after Hegseth survived the vote Tuesday evening, saying the vote was an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”
“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!” he added.
Hegseth, a former Fox News co-host, has been a polarizing figure in Washington, surviving a bruising Senate confirmation battle in 2025.
However, one GOP critic, outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said he has had plenty of disagreements with Hegseth but didn’t like how the impeachment resolution was led by Massie.

“I don’t really align with the impeachment itself,” Bacon, an Air Force veteran, told reporters before the vote. “But I surely, if you would have put in [a line] about firing 80 generals, if we talk about firing 80 generals and not spending appropriated money, I’d feel a little differently about it.”

Another Republican leaving Congress this year, Rep. Darrell Issa of California, suggested Massie was pushing impeachment because he was upset about his primary defeat. And he added that even if it did pass the House, there are not 67 senators who would vote to convict him in a Senate trial.

“It’s going to die in the Senate; it’s just that simple. It doesn’t really matter what happens in the House. The secretary has committed no high crimes or misdemeanors,” Issa said. “The Senate often has to protect against the rashness of the House.”
Massie’s resolution included eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.
The first article charges Hegseth “with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat,” according to Massie.

Three others that are related to Iran fault Hegseth with continuing the war after both the House and Senate directed the removal of U.S. forces; continuing hostilities after the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period had expired; and ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties.

Another article charges Hegseth with directing “extrajudicial killings” of suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean, secondary strikes on survivors, and overseeing orders to U.S. personnel not to rescue shipwrecked persons.

The others say Hegseth illegally seized and deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro “to assert U.S. control over Venezuela’s oil reserves”; used the Defense Department to retaliate against and demote Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for telling service members they should not follow unlawful orders; and carried out an unlawful war in Yemen.

Hegseth on Tuesday morning defended his record and said every operation was a lawful one. “We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s the job well done,” he said.

title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
summary: NBC News projects that Salazar defeated her Democratic opponent in a heavily Hispanic, Miami-based district that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.
story: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after having clashed with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, tried to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”
But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns about impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview in which García told The Miami Herald, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the country. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.
Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.
In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
summary: How an NBC News data investigation tracked vaccination and school exemption rates across thousands of counties in the U.S.
story: Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.
For Subscribers

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.
Methodology

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.
The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.
For Subscribers
After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:
Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful.
Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions.

MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates.
Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.
With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.All data was checked for accuracy.
Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.
Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.
All data was checked for accuracy.

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers. In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.

Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers.

In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.

Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.
Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.

Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.

title: Woman apologizes for making racist gestures outside Ole Miss students’ apartment
summary: The University of Mississippi is investigating the incident after a video caught two women mimicking apes outside three Black students’ front door.
story: One of the two young women seen on a viral video making racist gestures outside the apartment of three Black Ole Miss students apologized for her actions.

Alaina Kunes, 18, said in a statement Tuesday that she did not know the people who lived in the apartment and was “unaware of their race” until the Ring doorbell camera video that captured the moment Friday gained national attention.

The video shows Kunes and two other women walking by the front door of the off-campus apartment where the three Black Ole Miss students live. Kunes is seen beating her chest. She and a second woman, who has not been identified and has not commented on the incident, make ape noises. A third woman in the video just walks by without stopping at the door.
“To the women I offended and to the Ole Miss community, I sincerely apologize,” Kunes said in her statement. “I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful.”
Kunes said she apologized to the women who live in the apartment directly. “I pray they will forgive me,” she said.

“I can never truly understand the pain I have caused them and it was never my intention. These girls deserve to feel seen and understood and what I did is not a reflection of who I am trying to become,” Kunes said.
The University of Mississippi launched an investigation into the incident, Shawnboda Mead, the school’s vice chancellor for student affairs, said in an email sent to the campus Sunday.
In it, Mead described the viral video as “showing University of Mississippi students engaging in racist gestures directed toward other students.”
Kunes has since withdrawn from the university, a source close to the 18-year-old told NBC News. It’s unclear what the enrollment status is of the other women in the video.
The University of Mississippi did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Tasha Bolton, the mother of one of the three Black Ole Miss students, wrote about the incident in a Facebook post Saturday. Bolton said her daughter is a freshman at the university and lives in the off-campus apartment with two Black roommates. She described the women filmed on the doorbell camera as her daughter’s upstairs neighbors.

“This is absolutely disgusting and unacceptable. College is supposed to be a place where young adults can learn, grow, and feel safe,” Bolton said about the video in her post. “We want answers. Specifically, what steps will be taken to address this behavior and ensure accountability?”
Kunes said she intends to fully cooperate with the university’s investigation.

“I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color,” she said in her statement apologizing for the incident. “I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal.”
Kunes also requested privacy for herself and her family and alleged that they have been harassed over the past several days and received death threats.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Mississippi is also looking into complaints it has received about the incident, Candi Richardson, the organization’s director of communications and community engagement, said Monday.

The most exciting part is that many of these meal kits are available at a great value, with some starting at as little as $25. If your family doesn’t love spending hours in the kitchen or you’re trying to keep this season’s big dinner below a certain cost without missing out on your favorites, these meal kits are perfect for you.

The best Thanksgiving meal kits in 2026

With grocery prices increasing due to inflation, going with a pre-made meal kit is a great way to be strategic. Individual categories, like produce and meat, poultry and eggs have all increased compared to Sept. 2025, so the same exact ingredients you bought this time last year will be higher overall.

These meal kits and grocery bundles could save you time and money. Many of them, including Walmart, Costco and Sam’s Club, also offer loyalty programs that could help you earn rewards on your future purchases.

This Thanksgiving meal kit from Walmart is one of the most popular options available, largely because it is the most affordable meal kit you can buy. All together, the grocery bundle costs $35, but you can save even more. Use promo code TRIPLE10 at checkout to get $10 off your order.
